📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Power Platform is Microsoft's low-code suite — five products that combine to handle business apps, automation, analytics, chatbots, and websites. The PL-100 exam tests your understanding of how the pieces fit together, when to use each tool, and how data flows between them. Get the big picture right and the rest of the exam becomes much easier.

The five products of Power Platform

ProductWhat it doesWhen to use
Power AppsBuild custom business apps with low-codeReplace paper forms, simple data-entry apps, dashboards
Power AutomateAutomate workflows (cloud + desktop)Approval flows, scheduled tasks, RPA, integrations
Power BIAnalytics and data visualizationDashboards, reports, exec summaries
Power PagesExternal-facing websites (formerly Power Apps Portals)Customer / vendor / partner portals
Power Virtual Agents (Copilot Studio)Build chatbots without codeFAQ bots, ticket triage, customer service
★ PL-100 EXAM TIP

Power Virtual Agents has been rebranded to Microsoft Copilot Studio (2023+). Some PL-100 exam questions still use the old name. Both refer to the same chatbot-building product.

The unifying layer: Dataverse

DATAVERSE = THE SHARED DATABASE
All five Power Platform products can read from and write to Microsoft Dataverse, a cloud-based database designed for business data.

Why it matters: One source of truth. Build an app in Power Apps, automate a flow in Power Automate, visualize in Power BI — all working off the same Dataverse data, no duplication.

Dataverse provides:
  Tables (similar to SQL tables / SharePoint lists, but enterprise-grade)
  Built-in security at the row/column level
  Auditing, business rules, calculated fields
  Native relationships between tables

Connectors — the bridge to everything else

Power Platform has 1000+ connectors — pre-built integrations to other services. Examples:

  • Microsoft 365: Outlook, SharePoint, Excel, OneDrive, Teams
  • Cloud services: Azure, AWS, Salesforce, Google Drive, Dropbox
  • Social/comms: Twitter, Slack, Gmail
  • Industry-specific: SAP, ServiceNow, Adobe Sign, DocuSign
STANDARD vs PREMIUM CONNECTORS
Standard connectors: included in basic Microsoft 365 licenses (SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, etc.).

Premium connectors: require a Power Apps per-app or per-user license. Examples: Salesforce, SQL Server, Dataverse (yes — Dataverse is premium!), Azure SQL, MySQL, custom connectors.

Cost trap on PL-100: questions often test whether a given scenario needs a premium license. Memorize: Dataverse = premium, SQL Server = premium, SharePoint = standard.

AI Builder — embedded AI

AI BUILDER
Drop-in AI models you can add to Power Apps and Power Automate flows. No data science background needed.

Pre-built models:
  Business card reader — extract contacts from photos
  Receipt processor — extract line items from receipts
  Invoice processor — extract invoice details
  Text recognition (OCR) — text from images
  Object detection — find objects in images
  Sentiment analysis — detect emotion in text
  Language detection — what language is this text?

Custom models: train form processors and prediction models on your own data.

Requires AI Builder credits (separate from Power Apps license).

The Power Platform ecosystem

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A typical Power Platform solution

Scenario: A retail company wants to manage in-store inventory checks by store associates.

  1. Power Apps (canvas): Associates use a mobile app to scan barcodes and enter counts
  2. Dataverse: Stores inventory records, counts, and history
  3. Power Automate: When count is below threshold, sends approval flow to manager for reorder
  4. Power BI: Manager dashboard showing low-stock items across all stores
  5. Copilot Studio: Customer-facing chatbot answers "Is item X in stock at store Y?"

All five products, all working off the same Dataverse data. This integration is why Power Platform exists — no single tool could do all of this alone.

Power Platform vs traditional dev

AspectPower PlatformTraditional development
Time to first appHours-daysWeeks-months
Who builds itBusiness users + "citizen developers"Professional developers
CustomizationWithin platform limitsUnlimited
HostingMicrosoft (cloud-only)Choose your own
Best forInternal business apps, automationPublic-facing products, complex logic

Governance and ALM (Application Lifecycle Management)

Power Platform admin features that the PL-100 expects you to know exist:

  • Environments: isolated workspaces (Dev / Test / Prod). Each has its own data and apps.
  • Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies: rules that block certain connector combinations (e.g., "no app can use Twitter AND SharePoint together") to prevent data leaks.
  • Solutions: packages that bundle apps, flows, and tables together for moving between environments.
  • Power Platform admin center (admin.powerplatform.microsoft.com): central management of environments, DLP, capacity, analytics.
⚠ COMMON PL-100 EXAM TRAPS

"Citizen developer": Microsoft's term for non-IT employees who build apps with low-code tools. Common in scenario questions.

"Solution" has a specific meaning: not "solving a problem" — a Solution is a deployment package containing apps, flows, and components, used to move work between environments.

Dataverse for Teams ≠ full Dataverse: Teams gets a free, limited version (1M rows, single environment per team). Production needs full Dataverse with paid license.

Don't confuse Power Pages with SharePoint: Pages is external-facing (anonymous + authenticated portals); SharePoint is internal-facing (Microsoft 365 users only).

Common PL-100 question patterns

"WHICH PRODUCT FITS THIS SCENARIO?"
Most PL-100 questions begin with a business need. Map it to the right product:

"Automate sending an email when..." → Power Automate (cloud flow)
"Build a mobile app for field staff..." → Power Apps (canvas)
"Show executives a sales dashboard..." → Power BI
"Customers self-serve their orders..." → Power Pages
"FAQ chatbot on the company website..." → Copilot Studio
"Extract text from scanned receipts..." → AI Builder (inside Power Apps or Power Automate)
"Process 100 invoices nightly from SAP..." → Power Automate desktop flow (RPA)
★ ON THE PL-100

Question style: PL-100 uses scenario-based multiple choice. You'll see a 2-3 sentence business problem, then options like "Build a canvas app" / "Use Power Automate" / "Create a Power BI report" / "Use Copilot Studio."

Key clue words: "mobile" → canvas app; "approval" → Power Automate; "dashboard" → Power BI; "external users" → Power Pages; "chatbot" → Copilot Studio.

Trust the obvious answer: PL-100 isn't trying to trick you. If a scenario says "automate," the answer is Power Automate.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Power Platform = 5 products: Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI, Power Pages, Copilot Studio (formerly Power Virtual Agents)
  • Dataverse is the unifying database that all products share
  • 1000+ connectors integrate with M365, Azure, Salesforce, SAP, and more
  • Standard connectors (free with M365) vs Premium connectors (paid license required)
  • Dataverse and SQL Server are PREMIUM — common exam trap
  • AI Builder adds drop-in AI models to apps and flows
  • Environments isolate Dev/Test/Prod work; DLP policies enforce data security
  • Solutions are deployment packages for moving work between environments
  • Map scenarios to products by clue words: mobile→Power Apps, automate→Power Automate, dashboard→Power BI, external users→Power Pages, chatbot→Copilot Studio

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The single biggest design decision in Power Apps: canvas or model-driven? This question appears in nearly every PL-100 scenario. Pick the wrong one and the app fights you the whole way. Knowing when to use each — and what each can/can't do — is a foundational skill the exam tests repeatedly.

Two fundamentally different approaches

AspectCanvas AppModel-Driven App
Design philosophyPixel-perfect, design-firstData-first, auto-generated UI
Layout controlTotal control, drag and drop anywhereStandardized templates, limited custom layout
Data sources200+ (SharePoint, SQL, Excel, Dataverse, anything)Dataverse ONLY
Best forMobile, task-specific apps, modern lookComplex data with relationships, CRM-style apps
ResponsiveYou configure for each form factorAutomatic — adapts to all screens
Building blocksScreens, controls, formulasTables, forms, views, dashboards
Maker effortHigher (design every screen)Lower (UI auto-generated from data)

Canvas Apps — design-first

CANVAS APP
Start with a blank screen. Drag controls (labels, buttons, galleries, forms) onto it. Write Excel-like formulas to wire behavior. Connect to whatever data source you want.

Think: PowerPoint meets Excel meets a mobile app builder.

Excellent for:
  Task-focused apps (inspection forms, time tracking, asset checkout)
  Mobile-first apps where layout matters (field worker apps)
  Apps that need to look polished and on-brand
  Cases where data is in SharePoint, SQL, Excel, or external systems 
// Canvas App structure (mental model):
App
├── Screen1 (Login)
│ ├── Label "Welcome"
│ ├── TextInput (username)
│ ├── TextInput (password)
│ └── Button "Sign In"
├── Screen2 (Home)
│ ├── Gallery (list of items from a data source)
│ └── Button "Add new"
└── Screen3 (Detail)
 └── Form (edit one record)

// Each control has properties (Text, Fill, Visible, OnSelect, Items)
// Wire them with Power Fx formulas:
Button.OnSelect = Navigate(Screen2)
Gallery.Items = SortByColumns(Tickets, "Created", Descending)
Form.Item = Gallery.Selected
Label.Text = "Hello, " & User().FullName

Model-Driven Apps — data-first

MODEL-DRIVEN APP
Start with your Dataverse data model (tables and relationships). Power Apps auto-generates a UI on top: forms to edit records, views to browse them, dashboards to summarize.

Think: Dynamics 365 / CRM-style app. Standardized look. Heavy data with relationships.

Excellent for:
  Complex business processes (sales pipelines, case management, project tracking)
  Apps where many users edit related data across many tables
  Cases where consistency and built-in security matter more than custom design
  Multi-device apps that need automatic responsive behavior 
// Model-driven app structure:
App
├── Sitemap (navigation menu)
│ ├── Group: Sales
│ │ ├── Tables: Accounts, Contacts, Opportunities
│ │ └── Dashboards: Pipeline Overview
│ └── Group: Service
│ ├── Tables: Cases, Knowledge Articles
│ └── Dashboards: Case Resolution
│
└── Components per Table (Dataverse-driven)
 ├── Forms (Main, Quick Create, Quick View)
 ├── Views (Active Cases, My Open Items, Closed Today)
 ├── Charts (Pipeline by Stage, Cases by Owner)
 └── Business Process Flows (guided stages)

// You don't design screens. You design the DATA MODEL.
// The UI is generated. Customize forms/views, but the layout pattern is fixed.

Decision matrix — which to pick

▸ WHEN TO USE EACH (PL-100 scenarios)
ScenarioPick
"Mobile app for field inspectors to take photos and submit forms"Canvas (mobile, custom UI)
"CRM for sales team tracking accounts, contacts, opportunities"Model-driven (complex relational data)
"Quick form to capture conference attendee info into SharePoint"Canvas (data in SharePoint, not Dataverse)
"Case management with auditing, security roles, and workflow"Model-driven (enterprise data needs)
"Custom-branded customer-facing event check-in app"Canvas (pixel-perfect design needed)
"Internal app for HR to manage employee data with departments and managers"Model-driven (relational HR data)

Key clue words on the exam

CANVAS APP CLUES
"mobile", "tablet", "field workers", "custom design", "branded", "pixel-perfect"
"SharePoint list", "Excel file", "non-Dataverse data"
"specific task", "single workflow", "barcode scanner", "camera"
"consumer-friendly", "kiosk", "simple data entry"
MODEL-DRIVEN APP CLUES
"CRM", "case management", "service portal", "Dynamics 365-style"
"complex data model", "many tables with relationships", "auditing required"
"multiple security roles", "business process with stages"
"responsive across devices automatically", "standardized UI"
"Dataverse" (specifically mentioned as the data store)

What you CAN'T do in each type

Can't do in CanvasCan't do in Model-Driven
Easy security at the row level (must code it)Use any data source other than Dataverse
Auto-generate UI from data schemaCustom pixel-perfect layouts
Built-in business process flowsUse external/SharePoint/SQL as primary data
Built-in auditing/historyMobile-first/kiosk experience easily

The third option: Custom Pages (hybrid)

CUSTOM PAGES — BEST OF BOTH
Newer capability (2022+): embed a canvas page inside a model-driven app. Lets you get model-driven app's data integration + canvas's custom UI for specific screens.

Example: model-driven app for case management with one custom canvas page that shows a custom dashboard with charts and KPIs that the standard model-driven dashboard can't render.

PL-100 mentions custom pages but doesn't test deeply on them. Knowing they exist is enough.

App design starting points

Starting pointResult
Blank appEmpty canvas, you build from scratch
Start from data (SharePoint, Excel, SQL, Dataverse)Canvas app with browse / view / edit screens auto-generated
Start from template (35+ available)Pre-built canvas app for common scenarios (Inspection, Inventory, etc.)
Start from page designPre-built layouts (sidebar, dashboard, gallery)
Power Pages siteExternal-facing website (different product)
⚠ COMMON PL-100 EXAM TRAPS

"Build a CRM app" → model-driven, not canvas. CRM is the classic model-driven scenario.

"Data is in SharePoint" → canvas only. Model-driven CANNOT use SharePoint as primary data.

"Need to scan a barcode with phone camera" → canvas. Model-driven doesn't offer easy device hardware access.

"Need business process flow with stages" → model-driven. Canvas doesn't have native BPF.

"Need auditing of who edited what" → model-driven. Dataverse provides built-in auditing.

Don't pick canvas just because it's "easier". If question describes complex relational data, model-driven is correct.

★ ON THE PL-100

"Which app type for [mobile data entry on the go]?" → Canvas

"Which app type for [CRM / case management / many tables]?" → Model-driven

"Model-driven requires what data source?" → Dataverse (always)

"Canvas works with what data sources?" → Any (200+ connectors)

"Built-in business process flows?" → Model-driven feature

"Pixel-perfect mobile UI?" → Canvas only

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Canvas = design-first, pixel-perfect, any data source
  • Model-driven = data-first, Dataverse only, auto-generated UI
  • Canvas wins for: mobile, custom design, non-Dataverse data, simple task-focused apps
  • Model-driven wins for: CRM-style data, multiple related tables, auditing, security roles, business process flows
  • Model-driven REQUIRES Dataverse — no SharePoint, no SQL Server
  • Canvas can use 200+ connectors including Dataverse, SharePoint, SQL, Excel, anything
  • Custom Pages (hybrid) embed canvas pages inside model-driven apps for the best of both
  • On the exam: keyword "mobile" → canvas; keyword "CRM/relational data" → model-driven

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Licensing trips up most PL-100 candidates. The exam has many "which license does this scenario need?" questions, and the wrong choice can cost real organizations thousands of dollars. Environments are equally critical — they're the boundary for security, data, and ALM (dev/test/prod). Get these two right and you'll handle the platform-governance section confidently.

Power Apps licensing

LicenseWhat you getPricing (2025)
Microsoft 365 (built-in)Run apps that use STANDARD connectors only (SharePoint, Excel, Outlook). No Dataverse, no SQL.Included with M365 E1/E3/E5, Business Basic/Standard/Premium
Power Apps per AppRun 1 (later: 2) specific app per user with premium connectors + Dataverse~$5/user/month per app
Power Apps per UserRun unlimited apps per user with all premium features~$20/user/month
Power Apps Developer PlanFree individual plan for learning/dev — full features, single user, no production useFree
Dynamics 365Bundled Power Apps capabilities for customers using Sales/Service/Field ServiceVaries by D365 SKU
LICENSE PICKER (PL-100 style)
"User only needs ONE specific custom app" → Power Apps per App
"User needs to use MANY custom apps" → Power Apps per User
"App uses only SharePoint / Outlook / Excel" → M365 (built-in) is enough
"App uses Dataverse or SQL Server" → Power Apps per App or per User REQUIRED
"Solo dev wants to learn and prototype" → Developer Plan (free)
"Sales team using sales pipeline app" → Dynamics 365 (likely already licensed)

Standard vs Premium connectors

CONNECTORS THAT REQUIRE PREMIUM LICENSE
If your app uses ANY of these, all users need a Power Apps license:

  Dataverse (yes, surprising — but it's premium)
  SQL Server (Azure SQL, on-prem SQL Server)
  Salesforce
  Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL
  SAP, ServiceNow, Workday
  HTTP / Custom connectors
  Adobe Sign, DocuSign
  Twilio

STANDARD (no extra license needed):
  SharePoint, Outlook, Excel, OneDrive, Teams
  Planner, OneNote, Forms, Stream
  Approvals (the built-in M365 one)

Environments — what they are

ENVIRONMENT
An environment is an isolated container in Power Platform. Each has:
  Its own Dataverse database (or none)
  Its own apps, flows, chatbots, AI models
  Its own users and security roles
  Its own connections to external systems

Think of an environment like a separate "tenant within a tenant."

An organization typically has multiple environments to separate concerns:
  Dev (build new things)
  Test (QA testing)
  Production (real users)
  Sandbox (experiments, training)

Environment types

TypePurposeNotes
DefaultOne per tenant, auto-created. All users can create apps here.Can NOT be deleted. Often a mess — limit serious work elsewhere.
ProductionReal business work, deployed apps for end users.Backed up automatically. Cannot be reset.
SandboxTest, dev, training. Cheaper. Can reset (wipe and start over).Can be copied from production for realistic testing.
Trial30-day free trial for evaluation.Expires automatically. Limited capacity.
DeveloperSingle-user free environment for individual learning.Comes with Developer Plan license.
TeamsAuto-created when you add a Power App to a Teams channel.Lightweight Dataverse for Teams (limited).

Environment lifecycle

// Typical environment progression for an enterprise app:

[Developer Plan] ← Personal sandbox for prototyping
 ↓
[Sandbox: Dev] ← Build the real app, iterate
 ↓ (export Solution)
[Sandbox: Test] ← QA validates, fixes bugs
 ↓ (export Solution)
[Production] ← End users use it
 ↓
[Sandbox: Hotfix] ← Copied from prod for fixing bugs without disrupting users

// Moving apps between environments uses SOLUTIONS (packaged deployments).

Solutions — packaging apps for deployment

SOLUTION
A solution is a container that bundles related Power Platform components — apps, flows, tables, business rules, security roles, environment variables — into one deployable unit.

Use solutions to move work between environments (dev → test → prod).

Two types:
  Unmanaged: source-code-like, editable. Used in dev environments.
  Managed: read-only, deployed to prod. Like compiled code. Updates by deploying newer managed solution.

Each solution has a publisher and a prefix (e.g., "contoso_") which is added to custom tables/columns so they're identifiable.

Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies

DLP POLICY
An admin-defined rule that blocks certain connector combinations to prevent data leaks.

Connectors get classified into groups:
  Business (trusted: SharePoint, Outlook, internal SQL)
  Non-Business (untrusted: Twitter, Facebook, Gmail)
  Blocked (cannot be used at all)

Rule: an app or flow CANNOT use connectors from different groups in the same app.

Example: a DLP policy puts SharePoint in "Business" and Twitter in "Non-Business." Now no one can build a flow that reads internal SharePoint data and posts it to Twitter — that data leak is prevented.

Sharing apps

Share withMechanism
Specific users / security groupsShare button on the app — User can run; Co-owner can edit
Microsoft 365 groupsShare with the group; members get access
Whole organization ("everyone in tenant")Share with "Everyone" — requires admin permission usually
External users (guests)Possible but requires Azure AD B2B; complex
Embed in TeamsAdd app to Teams channel/tab; team members get access

Permission levels on a canvas app

RoleCan do
UserRun the app
Co-ownerRun, edit, share with others (NOT delete or change owner)
OwnerAll the above + delete + change owner
⚠ COMMON PL-100 EXAM TRAPS

"User wants to run a Power App with Dataverse data" → needs Power Apps per App / per User, NOT just M365. Dataverse is premium.

"Need to test changes before users see them" → use sandbox environment, deploy via solution after testing.

"Prevent users from creating apps that connect SharePoint and Gmail together" → DLP policy with SharePoint in Business and Gmail in Non-Business.

"Default environment cannot be deleted" — common factual question.

"Production environment cannot be RESET" — only sandbox can.

"Move app from dev to prod" → export as managed solution, import to prod.

Co-owner can't delete the app — only the owner can.

★ ON THE PL-100

"App uses Dataverse → license needed?" → Power Apps per App or per User

"App uses only SharePoint → license needed?" → M365 (no extra)

"How to deploy app dev → prod?" → Managed solution

"How to prevent data leak between connector groups?" → DLP policy

"How to test without affecting prod?" → Sandbox environment

"What's the default environment?" → Auto-created, can't delete, all users access

"Co-owner permission?" → Edit + share, NOT delete

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • M365 license = standard connectors only (SharePoint, Outlook, Excel)
  • Premium connectors (Dataverse, SQL, Salesforce, etc.) require Power Apps per App or per User
  • Power Apps per App = 1-2 specific apps; per User = unlimited apps
  • Developer Plan = free for individual learning, not production
  • Dataverse is PREMIUM despite being Microsoft-native
  • Environments isolate apps/data/users; common pattern: Dev / Test / Prod
  • Default environment cannot be deleted; production cannot be reset
  • Sandbox environments can be reset or copied from production
  • Solutions package apps/flows/tables for deployment between environments
  • Managed solutions = read-only, used in production; unmanaged = editable, used in dev
  • DLP policies block dangerous connector combinations to prevent data leaks
  • App permissions: User (run), Co-owner (edit), Owner (delete)

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Canvas apps are the most common Power Apps you'll build — pixel-perfect, drag-and-drop interfaces backed by formulas. They look like PowerPoint slides but behave like apps. The PL-100 exam tests canvas app structure, creation modes, and the maker portal.

Creating a canvas app

Go to make.powerapps.com → sign in with Microsoft 365 account

Three starting points:
 1. Start with data — pick a data source; Power Apps generates app
 2. Start with design — choose a template or blank
 3. Start with a Copilot — describe what you want; AI generates

Common templates:
 Tablet form factor (default; ~1366×768 landscape)
 Phone form factor (portrait; mobile-friendly)
 Blank canvas
 From SharePoint list
 From Excel table
 From Dataverse

Once created, opens in Power Apps Studio (browser-based editor)

Power Apps Studio interface

Browser-based editor with three panes:

Left side: Tree view
 - Lists all screens, controls, components
 - Hierarchy of the app
 - Add new screens, components, data sources

Center: Canvas
 - The screen being designed
 - Drag-and-drop controls here
 - Preview of what users see

Right side: Properties pane
 - Properties of the selected control
 - Two tabs: Properties (visual) and Advanced (all properties)
 - Format pane for styling

Top: Command bar
 - File menu (Save, Settings, Share)
 - Insert tab (add controls)
 - Data tab (data sources)
 - Action tab (formulas)

Formula bar:
 - Below the command bar
 - Edit any property's formula
 - Excel-like syntax (Power Fx)

App structure

App
 └─ Screens
 └─ Controls (buttons, labels, galleries, forms, etc.)
 └─ Properties (Text, Color, OnSelect, Visible, etc.)
 └─ Each screen has its own controls

 └─ Data Sources
 └─ Connections to SharePoint, Dataverse, Excel, etc.
 └─ Can be tables, views, or specific entities

 └─ Components (optional)
 └─ Reusable control bundles
 └─ Custom dropdowns, navigation menus, etc.

 └─ Variables (global, screen-level, collections)

 └─ Themes / branding

Screen aspect ratios

FormatDimensionsBest for
Tablet1366 × 768 (landscape)Desktop browser, iPad
Phone640 × 1136 (portrait)Mobile-first apps
CustomAny sizeSpecial use cases

Choose at app creation. To change later: File → Settings → Screen size + orientation.

The first screen

When you create a blank canvas app, you get Screen1
Default named "Screen1" — rename via tree view (right-click → Rename)

Rename screens with meaningful names:
 HomeScreen, DetailScreen, FormScreen, SettingsScreen
 Easier to navigate large apps

The App object:
 Has its own properties (e.g., OnStart formula)
 Set initial variables, load data, navigate to a default screen

Screen properties:
 Fill (background color)
 ImagePosition, Image (background image)
 Height, Width
 OnVisible (formula runs when screen becomes active)
 OnHidden (formula runs when leaving)
 ShowNavigationBar (set to false in mobile)

Saving and publishing

Save (Ctrl+S):
 Saves your work to the cloud
 Creates a new version
 Available immediately to you (the maker)

Versions:
 Each save = new version (numbered)
 Restore older versions via File → Versions

Publish:
 Save makes it accessible to YOU
 Publish makes it accessible to SHARED users
 File → Publish
 Confirm to publish to production

 Workflow:
 1. Edit and save (changes saved but not live for others)
 2. Test in your version
 3. Publish when ready

Save vs Publish distinction is important for shared apps:
 Saving doesn't break things for current users
 Publishing pushes changes to everyone

Run modes

Two ways to test:

 Preview (F5 or Play button):
 Runs inside the Studio
 Quick test
 All controls work
 Exits back to editing on Esc

 Run in browser:
 Opens app in browser as published version
 True production behavior
 Use to test pre-publishing

Production run:
 Via Power Apps mobile app
 Via app launcher (apps.powerapps.com)
 Via Teams (Apps tab) if shared there
 Direct URL link to the app

Settings to know

File → Settings

 General:
 App name, description, icon
 Author
 
 Display:
 Orientation (Landscape / Portrait)
 Aspect ratio
 Scale to fit (on/off — usually on for adaptive)
 Lock aspect ratio (on usually preferred)

 Updates:
 Enable Power Fx new features
 Performance settings

 Advanced settings:
 Auto-save, formula behavior
 Compatibility version

Auto-save and undo

Auto-save (recent feature):
 Off by default
 Enable in File → Settings → Upcoming features → Auto save

Undo / Redo:
 Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y
 Works on most changes
 Doesn't undo deletes of data, just edits

Note: changes within formulas are tracked in undo
But changes to data sources outside the app aren't undoable

Versioning

Every save creates a new version

File → Versions:
 See full history (date, author, changes summary)
 Restore: makes a chosen version current
 Useful if a bad change breaks the app

Best practice:
 Save frequently
 Comment your save (in newer versions)
 Test after each major change

Sharing the app

File → Share

Options:
 Specific users / groups by email
 Roles:
 Can co-author (edit)
 Can use (run only)

 Notify by email (sends link)
 Add a message

After sharing:
 Users can run via the Power Apps launcher
 Or via direct link
 Authentication uses Microsoft 365 sign-in

Sharing requires:
 App must be saved AND published
 Saved-only is invisible to others

Worked example — create a simple canvas app

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — From scratch
// Goal: Build a simple "Expense Tracker" canvas app

// Step 1: Create
// make.powerapps.com → + Create → Blank canvas app
// Name: "Expense Tracker"
// Format: Tablet (1366×768)

// Step 2: Rename Screen1 → "HomeScreen"
// Right-click Screen1 → Rename
// Screen properties: Fill = "#F8F9FA"

// Step 3: Add a title label
// Insert tab → Label
// Properties:
// Text: "Expense Tracker"
// Font: 28pt
// Color: RGBA(64,64,64,1)
// X: 40, Y: 40

// Step 4: Add a button
// Insert tab → Button
// Properties:
// Text: "New Expense"
// OnSelect: Navigate(NewExpenseScreen, ScreenTransition.Fade)

// Step 5: Add a second screen
// Tree view → +Add → New screen → Blank
// Rename to "NewExpenseScreen"

// Step 6: Save the app
// Ctrl+S
// First save prompts for name + environment

// Step 7: Test
// Press F5 (Preview)
// Click "New Expense" button → navigates to NewExpenseScreen
// Esc to return to editor

// Step 8: Publish (when ready to share)
// File → Publish

Common canvas app mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Confusing Save and Publish — Save persists for you; Publish releases to shared users
  2. Generic screen names (Screen1, Screen2) — rename for clarity
  3. Default tablet when phone is intended — choose at creation
  4. Editing live app without testing first — break for end users
  5. Forgetting to share after publishing — file → Share separately
  6. Auto-save off without realizing — work lost on crash
  7. Renaming break-formula references — Power Apps usually updates them but verify
  8. Wrong environment — defaults vary; check before saving
  9. Big formulas without breaking up — hard to debug
  10. No OnStart logic when app needs initialization
★ ON THE EXAM

"Authoring portal?" → make.powerapps.com

"Create a canvas app?" → make.powerapps.com → + Create → Blank canvas app.

"Two main form factors?" → Tablet (landscape) and Phone (portrait).

"Studio panes?" → Tree view (left), Canvas (center), Properties (right).

"Save vs Publish?" → Save persists for you; Publish releases to others.

"Test the app?" → F5 / Preview button.

"Run published app?" → Power Apps mobile / Apps launcher / Teams / direct link.

"Restore old version?" → File → Versions.

"Share with users?" → File → Share → add users + role.

"Initialize on launch?" → App.OnStart property.

"Screen background?" → Fill property.

"OnVisible vs OnStart?" → OnVisible runs each screen entry; OnStart runs once at app launch.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Canvas apps are pixel-perfect, drag-and-drop interfaces backed by Power Fx formulas
  • Built in Power Apps Studio at make.powerapps.com
  • Three panes in Studio: Tree view (left), Canvas (center), Properties (right)
  • Two form factors: Tablet (1366×768 landscape) and Phone (640×1136 portrait)
  • Start options: with data, with design, with Copilot, or blank
  • App structure: App → Screens → Controls; plus Data Sources, Components, Variables
  • Save (Ctrl+S) persists for you; Publish releases to shared users
  • F5 or Play button runs the app in Preview mode for testing
  • File → Versions shows save history; can restore older versions
  • File → Share adds users (Can co-author for edit; Can use for run-only)
  • App.OnStart runs once at app launch; Screen.OnVisible runs on each entry
  • Rename screens immediately for clarity (HomeScreen, DetailScreen, etc.)
  • Auto-save is off by default; enable in File → Settings if desired
  • Run published app: Power Apps mobile / Apps launcher / Teams / direct URL
  • Always test in Preview, then Publish, then share — don't break live users

Controls are the building blocks of any canvas app — labels, text inputs, buttons, dropdowns, sliders, and more. Each has dozens of properties. The PL-100 exam tests recognizing common controls and their key properties.

Adding controls

Insert tab in command bar → categories of controls:

 Text:
 Label, Text input, HTML text, Rich text editor, Markdown viewer

 Input:
 Button, Dropdown, Combo box, Toggle, Slider, Rating, Date picker,
 Time picker, List box, Check box, Radio, Search box

 Layout:
 Container (modern), Vertical/Horizontal container, 
 Form (Edit and Display), Gallery (vertical, horizontal, layout-based)

 Media:
 Image, Camera, Microphone, Add picture, Video, Audio, Pen input

 Charts:
 Column, Line, Pie

 Icons:
 Hundreds of built-in icons (+, X, edit, save, etc.)

 Modern controls (newer):
 Modern Button, Modern Text input, etc. (cleaner styling)

Common controls in detail

Label

Insert → Label
Used for: titles, labels, dynamic text display

Key properties:
 Text — what's displayed (can be a formula)
 Font — font family
 Size — font size in points
 Color — text color
 Align — Left, Center, Right
 FontWeight — Normal, Bold, Light
 Italic — true/false
 Underline — true/false

Examples:
 Text = "Welcome, " & User().FullName
 Text = "Total: $" & Sum(Expenses, Amount)
 Text = Today() // displays current date

Text input

Insert → Text input
User-editable text field

Key properties:
 Default — initial value
 HintText — placeholder
 Mode — Number, Text, MultiLine
 MaxLength — character limit
 Reset — set true to clear value
 OnChange — formula runs when text changes
 
Accessing the entered value elsewhere:
 TextInput1.Text // the current text

Example:
 Button.OnSelect = Set(varName, NameInput.Text)

Button

Insert → Button
Triggers an action when tapped

Key properties:
 Text — button caption
 OnSelect — formula runs on tap (most important!)
 Fill — background color
 Color — text color
 BorderColor, BorderThickness
 RadiusTopLeft, etc. — rounded corners
 Disabled — true/false; greys out
 Visible — true/false; hides

OnSelect formulas:
 Navigate(NextScreen)
 Submit(FormName)
 Set(myVar, true)
 Notify("Saved!", NotificationType.Success)
 Patch(Source, Defaults(Source), {Name: "Alice"})

Dropdown and Combo box

Dropdown (single-select):
 Insert → Dropdown
 
 Properties:
 Items — table or list of values
 Default — initial selected
 Selected — currently selected item
 OnChange — formula when selection changes
 
 Examples:
 Items: ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"]
 Items: Choices(Expenses.Category) // from Dataverse choice column
 Selected: Dropdown1.Selected.Value // the picked value

Combo box (multi-select supported):
 Insert → Combo box
 
 Properties:
 Items — same as Dropdown
 SelectMultiple — true for multi-select
 SelectedItems — list of selected
 SearchFields — which columns to search
 
 Examples:
 SelectedItems: ComboBox1.SelectedItems // List of records

Toggle

Insert → Toggle
On/off switch

Properties:
 Value — true (on) or false (off)
 Default — initial state
 OnChange — formula on change

Usage:
 Toggle1.Value // boolean
 
Example formula:
 If(Toggle1.Value, "Active", "Inactive")

Slider

Insert → Slider
Numeric range input

Properties:
 Min, Max — range
 Default — initial value
 Value — current value
 Snap — snap to integers
 
Example:
 Slider1.Value // numeric output

Date picker

Insert → Date picker
Calendar input

Properties:
 DefaultDate — initial date
 StartYear, EndYear — allowable range
 Format — display format
 SelectedDate — current date
 Language — locale

Example:
 Patch(Trips, ..., { Date: DatePicker1.SelectedDate })

Property categories

Property typeExamples
VisualFill, Color, BorderColor, Font, Size
LayoutX, Y, Width, Height, Padding
BehaviorOnSelect, OnChange, OnVisible, OnHidden
StateDefault, Value, Selected, Reset
DataItems, ItemFormat, Filter, Sort

Properties pane modes

Right panel has two main tabs:

Properties tab:
 - Common visual properties (Fill, Color, Border, etc.)
 - Easy GUI editing
 - For style and basic config

Advanced tab:
 - ALL properties listed
 - Edit complex formulas
 - Most useful for behavior properties (OnSelect, OnChange)

Switch via tabs at top of right panel

Formula bar approach:
 Click any property name → formula appears in top formula bar
 Edit there (large, scrollable area)
 Save with Enter / Esc to cancel

Conditional visibility and behavior

Visible property:
 Set to a formula returning true/false
 Hides control when false (still takes space? NO — collapses)
 
 Example:
 AdminButton.Visible = User().Email = "admin@company.com"
 SaveButton.Visible = !IsBlank(NameInput.Text)

Disabled property (DisplayMode):
 DisplayMode controls interactivity
 Edit — fully interactive
 View — read-only, looks normal
 Disabled — greyed out, no interaction
 
 Example:
 SaveButton.DisplayMode = If(IsBlank(NameInput.Text), Disabled, Edit)

Color-changing logic:
 Fill: If(IsValid, ColorValue("#28a745"), ColorValue("#dc3545"))

Containers and grouping

Container controls group related items together

Two main types (modern):
 Vertical container — stacks children top-to-bottom
 Horizontal container — stacks children left-to-right

Properties:
 LayoutDirection
 LayoutAlignItems
 LayoutJustifyContent
 Gap (spacing between children)

Why use containers:
 - Keep related controls aligned
 - Responsive layouts (children resize together)
 - Easier to move groups around
 - Better for accessibility

Old-style:
 Just position controls absolutely (X, Y, Width, Height)
 Manual alignment; brittle

Container approach is now preferred for responsive layouts

Naming conventions

Default names: Label1, Button1, TextInput1, etc.
Better practice: rename with descriptive prefixes

Common convention:
 lbl — Label
 btn — Button
 txt — Text input
 ddl — Dropdown
 cmb — Combo box
 gal — Gallery
 frm — Form
 scr — Screen
 cmp — Component

Examples:
 lblTitle
 btnSubmit
 txtEmail
 ddlCategory
 galProducts
 frmEditExpense
 scrHome

Why rename:
 Formulas reference controls by name
 Many controls means it's easy to lose track
 Easier debugging and maintenance

Right-click control → Rename (or F2)

Worked example — login screen

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Build a login screen
// Goal: simple login screen with username, password, submit button

// Setup
// 1. Add a screen → rename to "scrLogin"
// Fill: ColorValue("#0078D4")

// 2. Add a Container (vertical) in center
// Width: 400, Height: 500
// X: (Screen.Width - 400) / 2
// Y: (Screen.Height - 500) / 2
// Padding: 40

// 3. Inside container, add:
// 
// Label "lblTitle"
// Text: "Welcome"
// Size: 32
// FontWeight: FontWeight.Bold
// Color: Color.White
// 
// Text input "txtEmail"
// HintText: "Email"
// MaxLength: 100
// 
// Text input "txtPassword"
// HintText: "Password"
// Mode: TextMode.Password
// MaxLength: 50
// 
// Button "btnLogin"
// Text: "Sign in"
// DisplayMode: If(
// IsBlank(txtEmail.Text) || IsBlank(txtPassword.Text),
// DisplayMode.Disabled,
// DisplayMode.Edit
// )
// OnSelect: 
// Set(varUser, txtEmail.Text);
// Navigate(scrHome, ScreenTransition.Fade)
// 
// Label "lblError"
// Text: ""
// Color: Color.Red
// Visible: Self.Text <> ""

// Test: F5; fill fields; click Sign in

Common control mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Forgetting OnSelect on buttons — button does nothing on tap
  2. Using static text in labels when dynamic is needed (use formulas)
  3. Wrong Mode on text input — Password mode hides input
  4. Dropdown without Items — shows empty
  5. Multi-select with Dropdown — use Combo box instead
  6. Default state confusion — Default sets initial; Value is current
  7. Containers not configured — controls don't auto-arrange
  8. Wrong X/Y coordinates — controls off-screen
  9. Naming conflicts — two controls with same name; formulas break
  10. Visible vs DisplayMode — Visible hides; DisplayMode disables
★ ON THE EXAM

"Display text?" → Label.

"User-typed input?" → Text input.

"Single-select list?" → Dropdown.

"Multi-select list?" → Combo box.

"On/off switch?" → Toggle.

"Pick a date?" → Date picker.

"Run formula on click?" → Button.OnSelect.

"Hide control conditionally?" → Visible property with formula.

"Grey out button?" → DisplayMode = DisplayMode.Disabled.

"Auto-arrange children?" → Container (Vertical or Horizontal).

"Properties pane tabs?" → Properties (visual GUI) + Advanced (all).

"Rename a control?" → Right-click → Rename (or F2).

"Convention?" → btnXxx, lblXxx, txtXxx, ddlXxx, etc.

"Display password masked?" → TextInput.Mode = TextMode.Password.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Insert tab in command bar groups controls by category (Text, Input, Layout, Media, etc.)
  • Each control has dozens of properties — visual, layout, behavior, state, data
  • Common controls: Label, Text input, Button, Dropdown, Combo box, Toggle, Slider, Date picker
  • Button.OnSelect is the most important property: formula runs on tap
  • Dropdown is single-select; Combo box supports multi-select and search
  • Properties pane has two tabs: Properties (GUI) and Advanced (all properties)
  • Containers (vertical/horizontal) auto-arrange children for responsive layouts
  • Visible property hides the control entirely (with formula evaluation)
  • DisplayMode controls interactivity: Edit, View (read-only), Disabled (grey)
  • Rename controls with prefixes for readability (btnSubmit, lblTitle, txtEmail)
  • Formulas in properties: type in formula bar; Power Fx evaluates them
  • Selected and Value properties return current control state
  • Default property sets initial state at app start
  • Modern controls (recently introduced) have cleaner styling than classic
  • OnChange formula runs when input value changes

Galleries and Forms are the two most important data-display controls in canvas apps. Galleries list records; Forms edit individual records. Together they enable CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) workflows. The PL-100 exam tests both heavily.

Galleries — list display

Gallery: scrollable list of records from a data source

Three layouts:
 Vertical gallery — stacked rows (most common)
 Horizontal gallery — side-by-side cards
 Blank gallery — fully custom

Templates (when adding):
 Title — single text per row
 Title + subtitle
 Image + title + subtitle
 Two columns / three columns
 Each is a starting point you can customize

Add:
 Insert tab → Gallery → choose layout

Bind to data:
 Items property → set to a data source or filter
 Examples:
 Items: Expenses
 Items: Filter(Expenses, Status = "Approved")
 Items: SortByColumns(Expenses, "Date", Descending)

Gallery structure

A gallery contains:
 - One TEMPLATE row (visible at top of gallery)
 - Tableau renders this template for each item in Items

Inside the template:
 Add controls like Label, Image, Icon, Button
 Reference ThisItem.[FieldName] to bind to data

Example template:
 Label1.Text = ThisItem.Title
 Label2.Text = "$" & ThisItem.Amount
 Icon1.Visible = ThisItem.IsImportant

Each rendered row uses ThisItem implicitly for that row's data

Selected item:
 Gallery1.Selected — the currently selected record
 Gallery1.Selected.Name — its Name field
 Useful in navigation and form binding

Editing gallery template

Click on a gallery → first row (template) becomes editable
Modify controls inside the template
Changes apply to every rendered row

Add controls to template:
 Tree view → expand Gallery → select template row → Insert control

Template properties:
 Visible — hides specific row conditionally (per row)
 Fill — color per row (alternating colors common)
 Height — auto or fixed

Conditional row formatting:
 Fill = If(ThisItem.Status = "Overdue", Color.Red, Color.White)

Gallery interactions

OnSelect (on gallery, not template):
 Runs when user taps any row
 Useful: navigate to detail screen

Example:
 Gallery1.OnSelect = Navigate(scrDetail, ScreenTransition.Cover)

Inside template:
 Each control can have its OWN OnSelect
 When user taps that control, fires that formula

Common patterns:
 Tap row → navigate to detail
 Tap delete icon → confirm and Remove
 Tap edit icon → navigate to edit form

Gallery1.Selected refers to the currently selected row
After Navigate, scrDetail can use Gallery1.Selected

Default and Selected

Default — gallery's initial selected row when shown
Selected — current selection

Both are records (not just IDs)

After Selected:
 Gallery1.Selected.Title — Title of selected
 Gallery1.Selected.Amount — Amount of selected

Used for:
 Form binding (form.Item = Gallery1.Selected)
 Conditional logic
 Detail page references

Forms — record editing

Form: pre-built control that handles editing a single record

Two types:
 Edit form — create or update; submit button needed
 Display form — read-only view

Add:
 Insert tab → Edit form (or Display form)
 Or "+ New" button when adding to gallery

Bind to data:
 DataSource property — which table/source
 Item property — which record (e.g., Gallery1.Selected)

Form auto-generates:
 Data cards (one per field)
 Each card has appropriate control:
 Text field → Text input
 Date field → Date picker
 Choice → Dropdown
 Boolean → Toggle
 Etc.

Customize:
 Fields button → choose which fields to include
 Reorder via drag

Edit Form workflow

Form modes:
 FormMode.New — creating a new record (blank)
 FormMode.Edit — modifying existing record
 FormMode.View — read-only display

Set the mode:
 Form.DefaultMode = FormMode.Edit
 Or programmatically: EditForm(Form1), NewForm(Form1), ViewForm(Form1)

Set the record to edit:
 Form.Item = Gallery1.Selected // edit selected row
 Form.Item = Defaults(Expenses) // create new with defaults

Submit form:
 SubmitForm(Form1) — saves changes to data source
 Form.OnSuccess fires after successful save
 Form.OnFailure fires on error

Reset form:
 ResetForm(Form1) — clears unsaved changes
 Forms have an Unsaved property — true if user has typed

Typical submit button:
 OnSelect = 
 SubmitForm(Form1);
 If(Form1.Unsaved = false, Navigate(scrList));

Data cards

Each field in a form is wrapped in a Data Card
 Data Card contains:
 Label (field name)
 Data control (text input, dropdown, etc.)
 Error message label
 Required indicator (*)

Customize a data card:
 Select the data card
 Properties pane: many options
 Required (* shown)
 Update formula — what value to save
 DisplayMode — for the entire card
 Visible — hide cards conditionally

Unlock card:
 Click "Advanced" → Unlock button
 Now you can edit the card's internal layout
 Adjust positioning, add custom controls

Updates and Saved values:
 Card.Update — formula evaluated on submit (what to save)
 DataCardValue1 — the inner control with the current value

Gallery + Form pattern (master-detail)

Most common canvas app pattern:
 Screen 1: Gallery of all records
 Screen 2: Form to view/edit a selected record

Implementation:

Screen 1 (scrList):
 Gallery (galExpenses):
 Items: Expenses
 OnSelect: Navigate(scrDetail, ScreenTransition.Cover)
 Add button:
 OnSelect: 
 NewForm(frmExpense);
 Navigate(scrDetail)

Screen 2 (scrDetail):
 Edit form (frmExpense):
 DataSource: Expenses
 Item: galExpenses.Selected
 DefaultMode: FormMode.Edit
 Save button:
 OnSelect: SubmitForm(frmExpense)
 OnSuccess (on form): Back()
 Cancel button:
 OnSelect: ResetForm(frmExpense); Back()
 Delete button:
 OnSelect: 
 Remove(Expenses, galExpenses.Selected);
 Back()

Three screens for full CRUD:
 scrList (read; navigate to detail or new)
 scrDetail (read/edit/delete)
 scrNew (create) — or reuse scrDetail with FormMode.New

Worked example — expense tracker

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — CRUD app
// Goal: Expense tracker with list and edit

// Data source: SharePoint list "Expenses" with columns:
// Title (Text), Amount (Number), Category (Choice),
// Date (DateTime), Status (Choice)

// scrList:
// Gallery galExpenses:
// Items: SortByColumns(Filter(Expenses, Status.Value <> "Archived"), "Date", Descending)
// Template:
// lblTitle.Text = ThisItem.Title
// lblAmount.Text = "$" & ThisItem.Amount
// lblDate.Text = Text(ThisItem.Date, "mmm dd, yyyy")
// Status icon: green/yellow/red based on Status.Value
// OnSelect: Navigate(scrDetail, ScreenTransition.Cover)
// 
// Button btnAdd:
// Text: "+ New"
// OnSelect: 
// NewForm(frmExpense);
// Navigate(scrDetail, ScreenTransition.Cover)
// 
// Search box txtSearch:
// HintText: "Search expenses..."
// OnChange: UpdateContext({searchQuery: txtSearch.Text})

// scrDetail:
// Edit form frmExpense:
// DataSource: Expenses
// Item: galExpenses.Selected
// // DefaultMode set by NewForm() or EditForm() button
// 
// Button btnSave:
// Text: "Save"
// OnSelect: SubmitForm(frmExpense)
// 
// frmExpense.OnSuccess: 
// Notify("Expense saved", NotificationType.Success);
// Back()
// 
// Button btnCancel:
// Text: "Cancel"
// OnSelect: ResetForm(frmExpense); Back()
// 
// Button btnDelete:
// Text: "Delete"
// Visible: frmExpense.Mode = FormMode.Edit
// OnSelect:
// Remove(Expenses, galExpenses.Selected);
// Back()

// Result: full CRUD app with master list + detail form

Common gallery and form mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Gallery without Items set — shows empty or "data source not set"
  2. Form without DataSource AND Item — can't submit
  3. Forgetting to call SubmitForm — changes not saved
  4. SubmitForm without Reset — old values persist for next record
  5. Editing template after navigation — confuses live behavior
  6. Gallery.Selected referenced before any selection — gets Blank()
  7. Sort doesn't work — wrong column or quotes around column name
  8. Filter doesn't update — formula doesn't depend on changing values
  9. Required fields in form not marked — submit fails silently
  10. Form unlock changes don't propagate — unlocked cards don't auto-update
★ ON THE EXAM

"List records?" → Gallery.

"Edit/create a record?" → Edit form.

"Read-only record view?" → Display form.

"Reference current row's field?" → ThisItem.FieldName (inside template).

"Currently selected row?" → Gallery1.Selected.

"Bind form to selected row?" → Form.Item = Gallery1.Selected.

"Save form changes?" → SubmitForm(Form1).

"After save action?" → Form.OnSuccess.

"Reset unsaved changes?" → ResetForm(Form1).

"Create blank record?" → NewForm(Form1) then SubmitForm.

"Edit existing record?" → EditForm(Form1) or set Mode = FormMode.Edit.

"View-only?" → ViewForm(Form1) or DefaultMode = FormMode.View.

"Delete a row?" → Remove(DataSource, recordToDelete).

"Form has unsaved data?" → Form.Unsaved (true/false).

"Filter the gallery list?" → Items = Filter(Source, condition).

"Sort the gallery?" → SortByColumns(Source, "Column", Descending).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Galleries display lists of records; the most common data-display control
  • Three gallery layouts: Vertical, Horizontal, Blank (custom)
  • Bind via Items property: data source, Filter(), Sort(), or any table expression
  • Inside a gallery template, reference current row's fields via ThisItem.FieldName
  • Gallery.Selected returns the currently selected row (a record)
  • Edit Forms create or modify records; Display Forms are read-only views
  • Form.DataSource sets the table; Form.Item sets which record to edit
  • Form modes: New (blank), Edit (existing), View (read-only)
  • Switch modes via NewForm(), EditForm(), ViewForm() functions
  • SubmitForm() saves changes to the data source
  • OnSuccess and OnFailure handlers fire after submit
  • ResetForm() clears unsaved changes
  • Data cards wrap each field in a form; each has Label + Data control + error label
  • Unlock data cards (Advanced tab) for custom layouts
  • Standard pattern: Gallery (list) + Form (detail) = full CRUD app
  • Remove() deletes a record from a data source

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Apps with multiple screens need clean navigation: how users move between screens, what they see during transitions, and how state is preserved. The PL-100 exam tests Navigate, Back, transitions, and navigation patterns.

The Navigate function

Navigate(Screen, Transition, UpdateContextRecord)

Examples:
 Navigate(scrHome)
 Navigate(scrHome, ScreenTransition.Fade)
 Navigate(scrDetail, ScreenTransition.Cover, {ItemID: 123})

Arguments:
 Screen — destination screen control
 Transition — animation style (optional)
 UpdateContext — optional record passing data via context vars

Transitions:
 ScreenTransition.None — instant; no animation
 ScreenTransition.Fade — cross-fade
 ScreenTransition.Cover — new screen slides in from right
 ScreenTransition.CoverRight — new screen slides in from left (reversed)
 ScreenTransition.UnCover — current slides out left
 ScreenTransition.UnCoverRight — current slides out right

Use cases:
 Navigate(scrDetail) on a Button OnSelect
 Navigate to form for edit: NewForm(Form1); Navigate(scrEdit)

The Back function

Back([Transition])

Returns to the previous screen
Uses the screen history stack (FIFO)
Optional transition override

Examples:
 Back()
 Back(ScreenTransition.Fade)

Useful in:
 Cancel buttons
 Done/back buttons on detail screens
 Modal dismiss

Notes:
 Back() doesn't reload state — same screen as you left it
 If users navigated deeply, Back() chains back through history
 Combine with ResetForm if you want to clear form state

Navigation patterns

1. Simple linear navigation

scrLogin → scrHome → scrDetail

Each screen has buttons that Navigate forward
Each screen has Back button or auto-back behavior

Pattern:
 scrLogin.btnSubmit.OnSelect = Navigate(scrHome)
 scrHome.galItems.OnSelect = Navigate(scrDetail)
 scrDetail.btnBack.OnSelect = Back()

2. Tab-style navigation

Bottom or top tab bar; tap to switch sections

Implementation:
 Reusable component or container at bottom of every screen
 Each tab button: 
 OnSelect: Navigate(scrTargetTab, ScreenTransition.None)
 Fill: If(App.ActiveScreen.Name = "scrTargetTab", Color.Blue, Color.Gray)

Or use the same icon-set approach:
 Home / Tasks / Profile icons in bottom bar
 Each Navigate to its own screen

3. Modal screens (overlay style)

For pop-ups: confirmations, settings, filters

Two approaches:
 A) Use Visible toggle on a container (modal overlay):
 Container.Visible = isModalOpen
 Open: Set(isModalOpen, true)
 Close: Set(isModalOpen, false)
 Container styled as semi-transparent overlay

 B) Navigate to a modal screen:
 Use ScreenTransition.Cover for a "popup" feel
 Navigate(scrModal)
 Back() on close

Approach A keeps state on same screen
Approach B easier for complex modal content

4. Drawer / hamburger menu

Side panel that slides in/out

Implementation:
 Container with X position controlled by variable
 Tab/swipe to toggle

Or:
 Use a component with built-in drawer behavior
 Many community templates available

Context variables vs Global variables

Global (Set)Context (UpdateContext)
Accessible from any screenOnly within the screen that set it
Set(myVar, value)UpdateContext({myVar: value})
Read: myVarRead: myVar (within that screen)
Use for: user info, app state, selected itemsUse for: screen-local flags, modal state
Persists across screensResets when leaving screen

Passing data between screens

Three options:

Option 1: Global variable
 Set(SelectedItem, gallery.Selected);
 Navigate(scrDetail);
 
 // On detail screen, reference: SelectedItem.Name

Option 2: Context variable (via Navigate)
 Navigate(scrDetail, ScreenTransition.Cover, 
 {ItemID: gallery.Selected.ID, Mode: "Edit"})
 
 // On detail screen, reference: ItemID, Mode

Option 3: Direct reference to source control
 // On detail screen, reference: gal_Home.Selected
 // No variable needed; works if user came from gal_Home
 // Brittle if multiple paths to same screen

Choose:
 Globals for important app-wide state (user info)
 Context for one-off screen transitions
 Direct ref for simple, single-path navigation

Conditional navigation

Navigate only if a condition is met:

 Button.OnSelect = 
 If(
 !IsBlank(txtName.Text),
 Navigate(scrConfirm),
 Notify("Please enter your name", NotificationType.Error)
 )

Validate before navigating:
 If(
 Form1.Unsaved,
 Notify("You have unsaved changes", NotificationType.Warning),
 Back()
 )

Or use:
 Confirm() function (modern Power Apps):
 If(Confirm("Discard changes?"), Back())

Screen-level state preservation

When user navigates away, Power Apps remembers each screen's state by default
 - Form values stay
 - Gallery selection persists
 - Variables remain

To reset on entry:
 scrHome.OnVisible = 
 ResetForm(frmExpense);
 UpdateContext({localVar: ""});
 // Any other reset logic

To reset on leave:
 scrHome.OnHidden = 
 Set(varSelected, Blank())

Common pattern: 
 Form screens use OnVisible to reset
 Detail screens preserve state for "back from edit" return

Notifications and confirmations

Notify(message, NotificationType, [Duration_ms])

Types:
 NotificationType.Success
 NotificationType.Information
 NotificationType.Warning
 NotificationType.Error

Examples:
 Notify("Saved successfully", NotificationType.Success)
 Notify("Error: " & ErrorMessage, NotificationType.Error, 5000)

Confirm dialog (modern):
 Confirm("Delete this item?")
 Returns true if user confirms, false otherwise
 
 If(Confirm("Are you sure?"), Remove(Items, ThisItem))

Display in app:
 Banner across top, auto-dismisses based on Duration_ms (default ~2-3s)
 Stacks if multiple Notify calls fire

Loading states

Long operations need user feedback (loading spinner)

Common pattern:
 Set(isLoading, true);
 // Long operation: ClearCollect, Patch large records, etc.
 ClearCollect(allItems, Filter(BigSource, condition));
 Set(isLoading, false)

Display loading state:
 Spinner control: Visible = isLoading
 Disable buttons: DisplayMode = If(isLoading, Disabled, Edit)
 Show progress label: "Loading..."

Power Apps native loading spinner:
 Insert → Icon → Loading (rotating circle)
 Animate via DisplayMode/Visible based on isLoading

For very long ops, consider:
 Power Automate flow (offloads work, faster response)
 Async patterns (advanced)

Common navigation mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Hardcoding transitions everywhere — pick one or two and be consistent
  2. No Back button on detail screens — user stranded
  3. Navigate without Set first — lose context of what was selected
  4. Global variables for everything — context vars are cleaner for transient state
  5. Forgetting to ResetForm on new entry — old data persists
  6. No loading feedback on slow operations
  7. Notify without proper type — generic info when error/success would be clearer
  8. Confirm dialog ignored result — must check return value with If()
  9. Deep stack navigation — user lost; consider top-level Home reset
  10. Auto-back via OS button not handled — Power Apps allows OS back; design for it
★ ON THE EXAM

"Switch screens?" → Navigate(ScreenName, Transition).

"Go back?" → Back([Transition]).

"Transition types?" → None, Fade, Cover, CoverRight, UnCover, UnCoverRight.

"Pass data between screens?" → Set() global, UpdateContext() local, or pass record via Navigate.

"Global variable?" → Set(name, value); accessible from any screen.

"Context variable?" → UpdateContext({name: value}); screen-only.

"Show notification?" → Notify(message, type).

"Confirm before action?" → If(Confirm("..."), action).

"Reset state on entry?" → Screen.OnVisible with reset logic.

"Loading spinner?" → Spinner icon with Visible bound to isLoading variable.

"Disable buttons during load?" → DisplayMode = If(isLoading, Disabled, Edit).

"Tab navigation?" → Navigate to tab screens; conditionally style active tab.

"Modal popup?" → Visible toggle on container OR navigate to modal screen with Cover transition.

"NotificationType values?" → Success, Information, Warning, Error.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Navigate(Screen, Transition, UpdateContext) moves between screens
  • Back() returns to the previous screen in history stack
  • Transition types: None, Fade, Cover, CoverRight, UnCover, UnCoverRight
  • Set() creates a global variable accessible from any screen
  • UpdateContext({var: value}) creates a screen-only context variable
  • Pass data via global vars, context vars (in Navigate's third argument), or direct control references
  • Screen.OnVisible runs each time the screen is entered — useful for resets
  • Screen.OnHidden runs when leaving the screen
  • Notify(message, type) shows a banner notification (Success/Info/Warning/Error)
  • Confirm("question") returns true/false based on user choice
  • Common navigation patterns: linear, tab-style, modal, drawer
  • For modals: Visible toggle on container OR Navigate with Cover transition
  • Validate before navigating: use If() with conditions
  • Loading spinners use a boolean variable bound to control Visible
  • Disable buttons during long operations to prevent double-clicks

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Power Fx is the formula language behind Power Apps. It's modeled after Excel — declarative, reactive, type-safe. Mastering Power Fx is what separates a basic app from a powerful one. The PL-100 exam tests syntax, common patterns, and recognizing what Power Fx CAN'T do.

What Power Fx is

Power Fx = Microsoft's low-code formula language

Characteristics:
 - Declarative (you state what; engine figures how)
 - Reactive (auto-recalculates when dependencies change)
 - Strongly typed
 - Type inference (rarely declare types explicitly)
 - Functional (function composition; no looping in traditional sense)
 - Excel-inspired syntax

Where used:
 - Power Apps canvas apps (most prominent)
 - Power Automate (expressions)
 - Power Pages (component logic)
 - Dataverse (column formulas)
 - Logic Apps (some expressions)

Excel users feel at home:
 IF, SUM, COUNT, VLOOKUP-like patterns
 Function names match many Excel functions
 Familiar approach for non-developers

Power Fx vs procedural code

Power FxTraditional code
DeclarativeImperative
Auto-recalculatesManually trigger updates
No traditional loopsfor, while loops
Use Filter, ForAll insteadIterate explicitly
No try/catchException handling built-in

Formula syntax basics

Property = expression

Each property of each control can be a formula

Examples:
 Label.Text = "Welcome, " & User().FullName
 Button.Visible = !IsBlank(NameInput.Text)
 Gallery.Items = Filter(Products, Category = SelectedCategory)
 Button.OnSelect = 
 Set(myVar, "value");
 Navigate(NextScreen)

Operators:
 +, -, *, / — arithmetic
 & — string concatenation
 =, <>, <, >, <=, >= — comparison
 &&, ||, ! — boolean (And, Or, Not)
 
Note: + does NOT concatenate strings; use & (Excel-style)

Data types

TypeExamples
Number42, 3.14, -100
Text (String)"Hello", "Alice"
Booleantrue, false
Date / DateTimeToday(), Now(), Date(2024,1,15)
ColorColor.Red, RGBA(255,0,0,1), ColorValue("#FF0000")
Record{ Name: "Alice", Age: 30 }
Table[{Name:"Alice"}, {Name:"Bob"}]
BlankBlank() — equivalent to null

Records and tables

Record: structured value with named fields
 {Name: "Alice", Age: 30, Email: "alice@example.com"}
 
 Access fields:
 rec.Name // "Alice"
 rec.Age + 1 // 31

Table: collection of records (one row each)
 [
 {Name: "Alice", Age: 30},
 {Name: "Bob", Age: 25},
 {Name: "Carol", Age: 35}
 ]

 Same as data sources (SharePoint list, Dataverse table)
 
 Operations on tables:
 Filter(tbl, condition)
 First(tbl), Last(tbl)
 Sort(tbl, column)
 AddColumns(tbl, "new", formula)
 Sum(tbl, column)
 CountRows(tbl)

Variables

Three types of variables in Power Fx:

GLOBAL VARIABLE:
 Set(name, value)
 Accessible from any screen
 
 Set(varUser, User().Email)
 Set(varTheme, "dark")
 
 Read: varUser

CONTEXT VARIABLE:
 UpdateContext({name: value})
 Only the screen that set it can read
 
 UpdateContext({isFormVisible: true})
 
 Read: isFormVisible (only on that screen)

COLLECTION:
 ClearCollect(name, table)
 In-memory table; same syntax as data sources
 
 ClearCollect(LocalItems, Items)
 Collect(LocalItems, {Name: "Diana", Age: 28})
 
 Read: LocalItems (as table)

When to use which:
 Set — user info, app state, simple values
 Context — screen-local UI state (modal open?, mode?)
 Collection — caching data; manipulating tables locally

Basic operators

Arithmetic:
 2 + 3 = 5
 5 - 2 = 3
 4 * 3 = 12
 10 / 4 = 2.5
 Mod(10, 3) = 1
 10 ^ 2 = 100

String:
 "Hello" & " " & "World" = "Hello World"
 "Total: $" & 100 = "Total: $100"

Comparison:
 5 = 5 → true
 5 <> 6 → true
 "Alice" < "Bob" → true (alphabetical)

Boolean:
 true && false → false
 true || false → true
 !true → false

Conditional (covered in detail later):
 If(condition, true_result, false_result)
 Switch(expr, case1, result1, case2, result2, default)

Function calls

Power Fx has hundreds of built-in functions
Call with parentheses, comma-separated arguments

Examples:
 Sum(Expenses, Amount)
 Filter(Products, Price > 100)
 Concat(Products, Name, ", ")
 Today()
 User().FullName

Function categories:
 Text: Concatenate, Left, Right, Mid, Upper, Lower
 Number: Sum, Average, Max, Min, Round, Ceiling, Floor
 Date: Today, Now, DateAdd, DateDiff, Year, Month, Day
 Table: Filter, Sort, GroupBy, First, Last, CountRows
 Logical: If, Switch, And, Or, Not, IsBlank, IsEmpty
 Behavior: Set, UpdateContext, ClearCollect, Patch, Submit Form

Compose by nesting:
 If(IsBlank(TextInput1.Text), "Empty", Upper(TextInput1.Text))

Multi-statement formulas

Use semicolons (;) to chain statements

Common in OnSelect properties:

 Set(varName, "Alice");
 Set(varEmail, "alice@example.com");
 Notify("Saved", NotificationType.Success);
 Navigate(scrHome)

All statements execute sequentially
The LAST expression is the result of the formula (rarely matters in behavior contexts)

Comments:
 // Single-line comment
 /* Multi-line
 comment */

Whitespace and newlines are ignored
Format for readability

The "behavior" vs "value" distinction

VALUE PROPERTIES:
 Return a value; evaluated continuously (reactive)
 Examples: Text, Items, Visible, Color, X, Y, Width, Height
 Don't call behavior functions (Navigate, Set) here

BEHAVIOR PROPERTIES:
 Run actions; triggered by events
 Examples: OnSelect, OnChange, OnVisible, OnHidden, OnStart
 Can use Set, Navigate, Patch, SubmitForm, etc.

Common confusion:
 Putting Navigate() in Label.Text → won't work
 Putting Notify() in Label.Text → won't work
 Putting "computed value" in Button.OnSelect → has no effect

Rule of thumb:
 If it CHANGES state or NAVIGATES, use a behavior property
 If it RETURNS a display value, use a value property

Reactive recalculation

Power Fx auto-tracks dependencies

Example:
 Gallery.Items = Filter(Products, Category = SelectedCategory.Selected.Value)

When SelectedCategory.Selected changes, Gallery.Items automatically re-evaluates
No need to call .refresh() or .update()

This is the "spreadsheet model":
 Cell A1 = 5
 Cell A2 = A1 * 2
 Change A1 to 10 → A2 auto-updates to 20

Same in Power Apps:
 Property values are formulas
 When dependencies change, value re-evaluates
 Everything stays in sync automatically

Common Power Fx mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Using + for string concat — use & (Excel-style)
  2. Navigate in a value property — does nothing
  3. Set in a value property — same problem
  4. Forgetting reactive nature — calculations auto-update; don't refresh manually
  5. Trying for loops — use ForAll, Filter, ClearCollect
  6. Comparing dates with = — = works for exact match; use DateDiff for ranges
  7. Treating Blank() as "" — they're different; use IsBlank() or IsEmpty()
  8. Calling Set on context vars — use UpdateContext instead
  9. Hardcoding values in formulas — extract to variables or settings
  10. Long formulas without breaking up — use Set to capture intermediate values
★ ON THE EXAM

"Formula language name?" → Power Fx.

"Inspired by?" → Excel (declarative, reactive, type-safe).

"String concatenation?" → & (not +).

"Comparison operators?" → =, <>, <, >, <=, >=.

"Boolean operators?" → &&, ||, ! (And, Or, Not).

"Global variable?" → Set(name, value).

"Context variable?" → UpdateContext({name: value}).

"In-memory table?" → Collection via ClearCollect / Collect.

"Multi-statement?" → Use ; to chain.

"Value property example?" → Text, Items, Visible, Color.

"Behavior property example?" → OnSelect, OnChange, OnVisible.

"Empty value?" → Blank() — check with IsBlank.

"Excel-style logical?" → If(condition, true, false); Switch(expr, case, result, default).

"Record syntax?" → {Field1: value, Field2: value}.

"Table syntax?" → [{record1}, {record2}, ...].

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Power Fx is Microsoft's low-code formula language, inspired by Excel
  • Declarative + reactive: you describe what; Power Fx auto-recalculates dependencies
  • Use & for string concatenation, not + (which is arithmetic)
  • Operators: arithmetic (+, -, *, /), string (&), comparison (=, <>), boolean (&&, ||, !)
  • Data types: Number, Text, Boolean, Date/DateTime, Color, Record, Table, Blank
  • Records are {Field: value} objects; Tables are [{}, {}, ...] arrays of records
  • Three variable scopes: Set (global), UpdateContext (screen), Collection (in-memory table)
  • Functions are called with parentheses and commas: Sum(Expenses, Amount)
  • Multi-statement formulas chain with ; (mostly in behavior properties)
  • Value properties (Text, Items, Visible) return display values
  • Behavior properties (OnSelect, OnChange) trigger actions
  • Don't put Navigate or Set in value properties — they're for behavior properties
  • Power Fx tracks dependencies automatically — no manual refresh needed
  • No traditional loops; use ForAll, Filter, ClearCollect for iteration patterns
  • Comments: // for single-line, /* */ for multi-line

Power Fx conversions: uppercase — Upper(s); text to number — Value("42"); the reverse is Text(42). Lower() and Proper() round out the case family — Value is how you convert text into a real number.

Power Fx has hundreds of functions, but only a few dozen appear in real apps. Knowing the common ones is faster than searching docs. The PL-100 exam tests recognizing which function to use for common scenarios.

Text functions

Concatenate / &:
 Concatenate("Hello", " ", "World") → "Hello World"
 "Hello" & " " & "World" → "Hello World"

Length and parts:
 Len("Power Apps") → 10
 Left("Power Apps", 5) → "Power"
 Right("Power Apps", 4) → "Apps"
 Mid("Power Apps", 3, 5) → "wer A"

Case:
 Upper("hello") → "HELLO"
 Lower("HELLO") → "hello"
 Proper("alice smith") → "Alice Smith"

Search:
 Find("Apps", "Power Apps") → 7 (position; 1-based)
 StartsWith("Hello", "He") → true
 EndsWith("Hello", "lo") → true

Trim and replace:
 Trim(" hello ") → "hello"
 TrimEnds(" hello ") → "hello" (same)
 Substitute("foo bar", "bar", "baz") → "foo baz"
 Replace("hello", 2, 3, "XYZ") → "hXYZo" (replace 3 chars starting at pos 2)

Split:
 Split("a,b,c", ",") → Table: [{Value:"a"}, {Value:"b"}, {Value:"c"}]
 Use with First/Last/Index for parts

Format text:
 Text(1234, "#,###") → "1,234"
 Text(Today(), "mm/dd/yyyy") → "10/15/2024"
 Text(3.14, "[$-en-US]$#.##") → "$3.14"

Number and math functions

Rounding:
 Round(3.7, 0) → 4
 Round(3.14159, 2) → 3.14
 RoundDown(3.7, 0) → 3
 RoundUp(3.2, 0) → 4
 Floor(3.7), Ceiling(3.2) → 3, 4

Absolute and sign:
 Abs(-5) → 5
 Sign(-5), Sign(5), Sign(0) → -1, 1, 0

Min/Max:
 Min(5, 3, 7) → 3
 Max(5, 3, 7) → 7
 Min(table, column) — works on table column too

Power and roots:
 Power(2, 10) → 1024
 Sqrt(16) → 4
 10 ^ 2 → 100

Mod:
 Mod(10, 3) → 1

Aggregations on tables:
 Sum(Expenses, Amount)
 Average(Sales, Total)
 Min(Orders, Date)
 Max(Customers, LastVisit)
 CountRows(filteredTable)

Date and time functions

Current:
 Today() — today's date
 Now() — current date + time
 TimeZoneOffset() — minutes from UTC

Build dates:
 Date(2024, 10, 15) — Oct 15, 2024
 Time(14, 30, 0) — 2:30 PM
 DateValue("2024-10-15") — parse string
 DateTimeValue("2024-10-15 14:30") — parse with time

Extract parts:
 Year(myDate), Month(myDate), Day(myDate)
 Hour(myTime), Minute(myTime), Second(myTime)
 Weekday(myDate) — 1 (Sunday) to 7 (Saturday)
 WeekNum(myDate) — week number of year

Arithmetic:
 DateAdd(Today(), 7, Days) — 7 days from today
 DateAdd(Today(), 3, Months)
 DateAdd(Today(), -1, Years)
 DateDiff(startDate, endDate, Days) — days between

Formatting:
 Text(myDate, "yyyy-MM-dd") — "2024-10-15"
 Text(myDate, "mm/dd/yyyy") — US format
 Text(myDate, "dddd, mmmm dd, yyyy") — "Tuesday, October 15, 2024"
 Text(myTime, "h:mm AM/PM") — "2:30 PM"

Common patterns:
 Last 30 days:
 Filter(Expenses, Date >= DateAdd(Today(), -30, Days))
 
 This month:
 Filter(Sales, Year(Date) = Year(Today()) && Month(Date) = Month(Today()))

Logical functions

Basic conditionals:
 If(condition, true_value, false_value)
 If(condition, value1, condition2, value2, default)

Examples:
 If(Score >= 60, "Pass", "Fail")
 If(IsBlank(Name), "Anonymous", Name)
 If(Age < 18, "Minor", Age < 65, "Adult", "Senior")

Switch (cleaner than nested If):
 Switch(
 expression,
 value1, result1,
 value2, result2,
 default
 )

Example:
 Switch(
 Region,
 "East", 100,
 "West", 150,
 "North", 200,
 0 // default
 )

And, Or, Not:
 And(a, b, c) — all must be true
 Or(a, b) — any must be true
 Not(condition) — negate

Equivalent:
 And(a, b) ≡ a && b
 Or(a, b) ≡ a || b
 Not(a) ≡ !a

Null/blank checks:
 IsBlank(value) — true if null or ""
 IsEmpty(table) — true if no rows
 IsNumeric(value) — is it a number?
 IsType(value, Type) — type check
 Coalesce(a, b, c) — first non-blank value

Table functions

Filter rows:
 Filter(Expenses, Amount > 100)
 Filter(Expenses, Category = "Travel")
 Filter(Expenses, Date >= Today() && Status = "Active")

Sort:
 Sort(Expenses, Amount)
 Sort(Expenses, Date, Descending)
 SortByColumns(Expenses, "Date", Descending, "Amount", Ascending)

First/Last/Index:
 First(table) — first row
 Last(table) — last row
 FirstN(table, 5) — first 5 rows
 LastN(table, 3) — last 3 rows
 Index(table, 2) — 2nd row (1-based)

Search:
 LookUp(Customers, ID = "C001") — first matching row
 LookUp(Customers, ID = "C001", Name) — value of Name field

Aggregate:
 Sum(Expenses, Amount)
 Average(Expenses, Amount)
 Min(Expenses, Date)
 Max(Expenses, Date)
 CountRows(Expenses)
 CountIf(Expenses, Category = "Travel")

Add computed columns:
 AddColumns(Products, "Total", Price * Quantity)
 Returns new table with extra column

Group:
 GroupBy(Sales, "Region", "RegionSales")
 Returns table with Region + nested table per region

Convert to text:
 Concat(table, formula, separator)
 Concat(Products, Name, ", ") → "Apple, Banana, Cherry"

Iteration: ForAll

No traditional for loop; use ForAll

ForAll(table, formula)
 Runs formula for each row
 Returns: table of formula results

Example:
 ForAll(Products, Price * 1.1)
 → Table of new prices (each row's price * 1.1)

For side effects (modifying data):
 ForAll(Items, Patch(MyTable, Defaults(MyTable), {Name: Name}))

Caveats:
 - Avoid ForAll for simple operations Filter/AddColumns can do (slower)
 - Use for explicit row-by-row operations
 - For mass updates, consider Patch with a record set

Data modification functions

Add record:
 Patch(Expenses, Defaults(Expenses), {Title: "Lunch", Amount: 25})
 
 Defaults() creates a blank record for the table
 Patch adds it; returns the saved record

Update record:
 Patch(Expenses, LookUp(Expenses, ID=5), {Status: "Approved"})
 
 Second arg: existing record to update
 Third arg: changes (only specified fields update)

Update multiple:
 Patch(Expenses, table_of_records, table_of_changes)
 Or use UpdateIf:
 UpdateIf(Expenses, Status = "Pending", {Status: "Approved"})

Delete:
 Remove(Expenses, recordToDelete)
 RemoveIf(Expenses, Status = "Archived")

Submit/reset forms:
 SubmitForm(Form1)
 ResetForm(Form1)
 
After submit, Form.LastSubmit refers to the saved record

App-level functions

User and environment info:
 User().FullName
 User().Email
 User().Image — user's profile picture URL

 Notify(msg, type) — show notification
 Confirm("Question?") — user confirmation dialog

 Reset(control) — clear a control's value

 Refresh(source) — fetch latest data from source

 Set(name, value) — global variable
 UpdateContext({n: v}) — context variable
 ClearCollect(c, table) — populate collection
 Collect(c, record) — add to collection

 Navigate(scrName)
 Back()
 Exit() — close the app

Date/time helpers:
 TimeZoneOffset() — minutes from UTC
 DateValue(string)
 DateTimeValue(string)

Math helpers:
 Pi() = 3.14159...
 Rand() = random 0-1
 RandBetween(1, 100)

Common function mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Using + for string concat — use & (Power Fx is Excel-style)
  2. Wrong argument count — most functions are strict about arg count
  3. Patch without Defaults() for new record — Patch needs base record + changes
  4. ForAll for what Filter does — Filter is faster
  5. LookUp expecting a list — LookUp returns one row; use Filter for multiple
  6. Sum without column — Sum(table, "ColumnName") not Sum(table.Column)
  7. Date comparison with = — works for exact match; use DateDiff for ranges
  8. Text(date, "MM") ambiguity — MM = month; mm = minutes
  9. IsBlank on numbers — 0 is NOT blank; check IsBlank for null/missing
  10. Forgetting Defaults() for Patch new record
★ ON THE EXAM

"Concatenate strings?" → & or Concatenate().

"Filter a table?" → Filter(table, condition).

"Sort a table?" → Sort or SortByColumns.

"Look up a single record?" → LookUp(table, condition[, returnField]).

"Sum a column?" → Sum(table, ColumnName).

"Count rows?" → CountRows(table) or CountIf for conditional.

"Add a row?" → Patch(table, Defaults(table), {fields}).

"Update a row?" → Patch(table, existingRecord, {changes}).

"Delete a row?" → Remove(table, record) or RemoveIf.

"Today's date?" → Today().

"Days between dates?" → DateDiff(start, end, Days).

"Add days?" → DateAdd(date, N, Days).

"User info?" → User().FullName, User().Email.

"First or last row?" → First(table), Last(table).

"Replace text?" → Substitute(text, old, new).

"Conditional?" → If(condition, true, false) or Switch.

"Iterate rows?" → ForAll(table, formula).

"Aggregate by category?" → GroupBy(table, "Column", "NestedTableName").

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Text: Concatenate (&), Left, Right, Mid, Upper, Lower, Substitute, Trim, Split, Text (format)
  • Math: Sum, Average, Min, Max, Round, Mod, Abs, Power, Sqrt
  • Date: Today, Now, Date, Year/Month/Day, DateAdd, DateDiff, Weekday
  • Format dates: Text(date, "format_string") with patterns like "yyyy-MM-dd"
  • Logical: If, Switch, And, Or, Not, IsBlank, IsEmpty, IsNumeric
  • Table: Filter, Sort, SortByColumns, LookUp, AddColumns, GroupBy
  • Aggregate: Sum/Average/Min/Max/CountRows/CountIf on tables
  • First, Last, FirstN, LastN, Index access specific rows
  • ForAll(table, formula) iterates rows; use sparingly
  • Patch: insert with Defaults(table) + changes; update with existing record + changes
  • UpdateIf, RemoveIf for conditional bulk operations
  • User() returns current user info (FullName, Email, Image)
  • Notify shows banner messages; Confirm shows dialog
  • Refresh(source) re-fetches data from source
  • Concat(table, formula, separator) joins values from a column
