Variables and collections are how Power Apps manages state. Choosing the right scope (global, context, collection) makes apps faster and easier to maintain. The PL-100 exam tests Set vs UpdateContext vs ClearCollect distinctions.

Three variable types

TypeFunctionScopeHolds
GlobalSet()Entire appSingle value or record
ContextUpdateContext()Single screenSingle value or record
CollectionClearCollect() / Collect()Entire appTable (multiple records)

Global variables: Set

Create / update:
 Set(varName, value)

Access:
 varName (anywhere in the app)

Examples:
 Set(varUserName, User().FullName)
 Set(varIsAdmin, User().Email = "admin@company.com")
 Set(varSelectedItem, Gallery1.Selected)
 Set(varTheme, "dark")

Best for:
 - User info needed across screens
 - App-wide state (theme, language, login status)
 - Selected/active items used in multiple places

Memory:
 Variables exist as long as the app session
 Reset when user closes/reopens app
 Initialize in App.OnStart for consistent startup

App.OnStart pattern:
 Set(varCurrentUser, User().Email);
 Set(varAppVersion, "1.0.0");
 Set(varTheme, "light");
 ClearCollect(colCachedItems, Items)

Context variables: UpdateContext

Create / update:
 UpdateContext({varName: value})

Access:
 varName (within the screen that defined it)

Note: takes a RECORD as argument
 UpdateContext({var1: value1, var2: value2}) — update multiple at once

Examples:
 UpdateContext({isFilterOpen: true})
 UpdateContext({selectedTab: "Profile"})
 UpdateContext({editMode: false, isLoading: true})

Best for:
 - Screen-local UI state (modal open?, mode flag)
 - Temporary data not needed elsewhere
 - Avoiding global namespace pollution

When user navigates away:
 Context variables RESET (re-initialized on re-entry)
 Use Screen.OnVisible to set initial values

Why use context over global:
 - Cleaner: don't clutter App-level state
 - Self-contained: screen owns its state
 - Performance: less memory tracking

Set vs UpdateContext — quick decision

Use Set (global) when:
 - User info (User().Email, FullName)
 - Selected item used across screens
 - App state (theme, language, login)
 - "Currently editing this record" (referenced by multiple screens)

Use UpdateContext (context) when:
 - Modal visibility (one screen's concern)
 - Tab selection within a screen
 - Form mode flag (Edit vs View)
 - Temporary form state before saving

Rule of thumb:
 If multiple screens need it → Global
 If only this screen needs it → Context
 When in doubt → Context (safer; cleaner)

Collections — in-memory tables

Create / populate:
 ClearCollect(colName, tableSource)
 Clears existing, then populates with source

 Collect(colName, recordOrTable)
 Adds to existing collection

 Clear(colName)
 Removes all rows (collection still exists)

Examples:
 ClearCollect(colCart, Defaults(Products)) // empty cart
 Collect(colCart, ThisItem) // add current item
 Collect(colCart, {Name: "X", Quantity: 1}) // add literal record
 ClearCollect(colCart, Filter(Products, IsInCart)) // copy filtered set

 Clear(colCart) // empty cart

Modify rows:
 Patch(colCart, LookUp(colCart, Name="X"), {Quantity: 2})

 Remove(colCart, recordToRemove)
 RemoveIf(colCart, Quantity = 0)

 UpdateIf(colCart, Discount, {Discount: 0.1})

Use as data source:
 Gallery.Items = colCart
 Same syntax as SharePoint or Dataverse

When to use collections

Best for:
 - Shopping carts (build before submitting)
 - Offline cache of remote data
 - Filtered/transformed snapshots of data
 - Temporary work tables (multi-step forms)
 - Aggregating data from multiple sources

NOT best for:
 - Long-lived data (use proper data source)
 - Large datasets (memory bloat)
 - Replacing the main data store

Memory considerations:
 Collections live in app memory during session
 Reset on app close
 Don't put thousands of rows unless necessary

Cache patterns:
 App.OnStart:
 ClearCollect(colProducts, Filter(Products, Active = true))
 
 Gallery uses colProducts for fast reactive UI
 Refresh button:
 ClearCollect(colProducts, Filter(Products, Active = true))

Working with records and tables

Create records:
 Inline:
 {Name: "Alice", Age: 30}
 
 As variable:
 Set(varPerson, {Name: "Alice", Age: 30})
 
 Access fields:
 varPerson.Name → "Alice"
 varPerson.Age → 30

Create tables (literal):
 [
 {Name: "Alice", Age: 30},
 {Name: "Bob", Age: 25}
 ]

 Or build with collection:
 ClearCollect(colPeople, [])
 Collect(colPeople, {Name: "Alice", Age: 30})
 Collect(colPeople, {Name: "Bob", Age: 25})

Records as variables:
 Set(varSelected, Gallery1.Selected)
 // Use anywhere as a record
 
 Update one field:
 Set(varSelected, Patch(varSelected, {Status: "Done"}))
 // Or just set explicitly:
 Set(varSelected, {Name: varSelected.Name, Status: "Done"})

Records on screens:
 After navigate, the variable carries the record
 Detail screen reads varSelected.Name, varSelected.Date, etc.

Initializing variables in OnStart

App.OnStart property:
 Runs ONCE when app launches
 Set defaults, load caches, prepare environment

Common pattern:
 // User info
 Set(varCurrentUser, User().Email);
 Set(varIsAdmin, User().Email = "admin@example.com");
 
 // App state
 Set(varCurrentScreen, "Home");
 Set(varTheme, "light");
 Set(varLanguage, "en-US");
 
 // Cache common lookups
 ClearCollect(colCategories, Categories);
 ClearCollect(colStatuses, Distinct(Items, Status));
 
 // Initial data fetch
 ClearCollect(colTopItems, FirstN(Items, 10));
 
 // Navigate to default screen
 Navigate(scrHome)

Avoid:
 Long-running operations in OnStart (app feels slow to load)
 If needed, use a "loading" screen with App.OnStart's last action being navigate

Resetting variables

Set to default:
 Set(varName, Blank()) — clear (treat as null)
 Set(varName, 0) — reset to zero
 Set(varName, false) — boolean default
 Set(varName, "") — empty string

Context vars:
 UpdateContext({varName: Blank()})

Collections:
 Clear(colName) — remove all rows
 ClearCollect(colName, []) — same; replace with empty

Logout pattern:
 Set(varCurrentUser, Blank());
 Set(varIsAdmin, false);
 Clear(colCart);
 Clear(colFavorites);
 Navigate(scrLogin)

Variable best practices

★ NAMING CONVENTIONS
Prefix conventions (community-driven):
 var — global variables (set via Set)
 loc — context variables (UpdateContext; "local")
 col — collections (ClearCollect)

Examples:
 varCurrentUser
 varIsLoading
 varSelectedRecord
 locModalOpen
 locFormMode
 colShoppingCart
 colCachedItems

Why:
 Easier to see scope at a glance
 Avoid name collisions
 Consistent across team

Avoid:
 Single-letter names (a, b, x)
 Vague names (data, item, value)
 Reserved words (Self, Parent, ThisItem)

Worked example — shopping cart

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Cart with collection

// App.OnStart
ClearCollect(colCart, []); // empty cart
Set(varCheckoutMode, false)

// Product gallery: galProducts

// CountIf(colCart, ProductID = ThisItem.ID) > 0,
// // Increment quantity if already in cart

// colCart,

// ),
// // Otherwise add new row
// Collect(colCart, {
// ProductID: ThisItem.ID,
// Name: ThisItem.Name,
// Price: ThisItem.Price,
// Quantity: 1
// })
// );
// Notify(ThisItem.Name & " added", NotificationType.Success)

// Cart screen: scrCart

// Gallery galCart:

// Template:

// lblQty.Text = ThisItem.Quantity

// btnRemove.OnSelect:

// // Submit to data source

// OrderDate: Today(),
// User: User().Email
// })
// );
// Clear(colCart); // empty cart after checkout
// Notify("Order placed!", NotificationType.Success);
// Navigate(scrConfirmation)

Common variable mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Using Set everywhere — pollutes global namespace; use UpdateContext for screen-only state
  2. Forgetting to initialize in OnStart — variable is Blank() until first Set
  3. Confusing Collect and ClearCollect — Collect appends; ClearCollect replaces
  4. Patch on a non-existent record — silently fails or creates duplicate
  5. Treating collection like list — collections are tables; need proper field access
  6. Storing huge data in collection — memory bloat; app slow
  7. Variable reset on screen leave — only for Context vars; Globals persist
  8. UpdateContext from another screen — only the screen that set it can read/update
  9. Iterating with ForAll modifying source — race conditions possible
  10. Naming variables identically to controls — confusion in references
★ ON THE EXAM

"Global variable?" → Set(name, value).

"Context variable?" → UpdateContext({name: value}).

"Multiple context vars?" → UpdateContext({a: 1, b: 2}).

"In-memory table?" → Collection via ClearCollect / Collect.

"Add to collection?" → Collect(name, record).

"Replace collection contents?" → ClearCollect(name, source).

"Empty a collection?" → Clear(name) (keeps the collection; removes rows).

"Initialize at startup?" → App.OnStart.

"Re-initialize on screen entry?" → Screen.OnVisible.

"Variable scope?" → Global = whole app; Context = single screen; Collection = whole app.

"Record syntax?" → {Field1: value, Field2: value}.

"Access record field?" → record.FieldName.

"Naming conventions?" → varX (global), locX (context), colX (collection).

"Clear all globals?" → Set each to Blank() individually.

"Save changes locally first?" → Use collection, then ForAll/Patch to data source on submit.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Three variable types: Global (Set), Context (UpdateContext), Collection (ClearCollect)
  • Global variables (Set) are accessible from any screen
  • Context variables (UpdateContext) are screen-only
  • Collections are in-memory tables; use ClearCollect to replace, Collect to append
  • Clear() empties a collection but keeps it; ClearCollect with [] does the same
  • Initialize app state in App.OnStart (runs once on launch)
  • Initialize screen state in Screen.OnVisible (runs each entry)
  • Patch updates / inserts records; Remove deletes
  • UpdateIf and RemoveIf for conditional bulk operations
  • Naming: var- (global), loc- (context), col- (collection) prefixes
  • Use collections for shopping carts, offline caches, temporary work tables
  • Don't store large data in collections — memory bloat slows the app
  • Records are { Field: value }; Tables are arrays of records
  • Access record fields with dot notation: record.FieldName
  • Context variables don't persist across screens — use globals if needed across

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real apps make decisions: show/hide controls, validate input, route navigation, format display values. Power Fx provides If, Switch, And/Or/Not, and several helper functions for null/empty checks. The PL-100 exam tests these directly.

The If function

If(condition, true_value, false_value)
If(c1, v1, c2, v2, ..., default)

Two-branch:
 If(Age >= 18, "Adult", "Minor")
 If(Status = "Active", Color.Green, Color.Red)
 If(IsBlank(Email), "Anonymous", Email)

Multi-branch (cascading):
 If(
 Score >= 90, "A",
 Score >= 80, "B",
 Score >= 70, "C",
 Score >= 60, "D",
 "F" // default
 )

Nested:
 If(
 IsAdmin,
 If(IsActive, "Admin (Active)", "Admin (Inactive)"),
 If(IsActive, "User (Active)", "User (Inactive)")
 )

Notes:
 Conditions evaluated top-down; first true wins
 No "fall through" like switch in C
 Last argument is default (no condition)

The Switch function

Switch(expression, value1, result1, value2, result2, ..., default)

Compares expression to each value; returns matching result

Example:
 Switch(
 Region,
 "East", 1000,
 "West", 1500,
 "North", 800,
 "South", 1200,
 0 // default if no match
 )

When Switch is cleaner than If:
 Comparing one value against many options
 Categorical mapping
 Avoiding repetitive If(x = a, ..., If(x = b, ...))

If vs Switch:
 Switch: compares EXACT values to one expression
 If: arbitrary conditions (>, <, AND, OR)

Mixing:
 Switch can have complex conditions in results
 But the comparison itself is equality on first arg

And, Or, Not

And(condition1, condition2, ...)
Or(condition1, condition2, ...)
Not(condition)

Equivalent symbols:
 And(a, b) ≡ a && b
 Or(a, b) ≡ a || b
 Not(a) ≡ !a

Examples:
 If(And(Age >= 18, HasConsent), "Allowed", "Denied")
 If(Or(IsAdmin, IsManager), AdminFeatures, BasicFeatures)
 Visible = Not(IsBlank(Name))

Short-circuit evaluation:
 Power Fx evaluates left to right
 Stops as soon as result is determined
 
 And: stops on first false
 Or: stops on first true

Multiple conditions:
 And(a, b, c, d) — all must be true
 Or(a, b, c, d) — any must be true

Mixing & and Switch:
 Switch(true, Score >= 90, "A", Score >= 80, "B", "F")
 Uses Switch with true as expression and conditions as cases
 Excel trick that works in Power Fx too

Comparison operators

=, <>, <, >, <=, >=

Examples:
 Age = 18 — exact equality
 Status <> "Done" — not equal
 Price < 100 — less than
 Score >= 60 — greater or equal

String comparison:
 "Alice" = "alice" → false (case-sensitive)
 "Alice" < "Bob" → true (alphabetical)

Date comparison:
 myDate = Today() — same date
 myDate < DateAdd(Today(), -30, Days) — older than 30 days

NaN and Blank:
 Blank() = "" → false (different types)
 IsBlank(Blank()) → true
 IsBlank("") → true (both treated as empty)

Power Fx caveat:
 Don't directly compare to Blank() with =
 Always use IsBlank()

Null and empty checks

IsBlank(value)
 Returns true if value is null, empty string, or Blank()
 
 IsBlank("") → true
 IsBlank(Blank()) → true
 IsBlank("hello") → false
 IsBlank(0) → false (zero is not blank)

IsEmpty(table)
 Returns true if table has no rows
 
 IsEmpty([]) → true
 IsEmpty(Filter(Items, false)) → true (no matches)
 IsEmpty(Items) → false (assuming has rows)

IsNumeric(value)
 Returns true if value is a number (or numeric string)
 
 IsNumeric(42) → true
 IsNumeric("42") → true
 IsNumeric("hello") → false

Coalesce(value1, value2, ...)
 Returns first non-blank value
 
 Coalesce(Blank(), "", "default") → "default"
 Coalesce(MyVar, "Unknown") — fallback pattern

Conditional formatting

Color, Visibility, DisplayMode based on conditions

Color examples:
 Label.Color = If(Amount < 0, Color.Red, Color.Black)
 
 Button.Fill = Switch(
 Status,
 "Active", Color.Green,
 "Inactive", Color.Gray,
 "Pending", Color.Orange,
 Color.LightGray
 )

Visible:
 Container.Visible = User().Email = "admin@example.com"
 ErrorBanner.Visible = !IsBlank(varErrorMessage)

DisplayMode:
 SaveButton.DisplayMode = If(
 IsBlank(NameInput.Text) || IsBlank(EmailInput.Text),
 DisplayMode.Disabled,
 DisplayMode.Edit
 )

Icon Type:
 StatusIcon.Icon = Switch(
 Status,
 "Active", Icon.Check,
 "Pending", Icon.Clock,
 "Error", Icon.Error,
 Icon.Help
 )

Input validation patterns

Required field validation:
 Button.DisplayMode = 
 If(IsBlank(NameInput.Text), DisplayMode.Disabled, DisplayMode.Edit)

Email pattern:
 Label.Visible = !IsMatch(EmailInput.Text, Email)
 // IsMatch returns true if input matches regex pattern
 // Email is a built-in pattern constant

Range check:
 ScoreError.Visible = 
 Or(Value(ScoreInput.Text) < 0, Value(ScoreInput.Text) > 100)

Required + format:
 Submit.DisplayMode = 
 If(
 And(
 !IsBlank(EmailInput.Text),
 IsMatch(EmailInput.Text, Email),
 Value(AgeInput.Text) >= 18
 ),
 DisplayMode.Edit,
 DisplayMode.Disabled
 )

IsMatch patterns:
 IsMatch(text, Email) — matches an email
 IsMatch(text, Match.Digit) — single digit
 IsMatch(text, "[0-9]{5}") — 5-digit zip
 
 Match constants:
 Match.Email, Match.Phone, Match.Letter, Match.Digit, etc.

Loops and iteration

No traditional for loops in Power Fx

ForAll for iteration:
 ForAll(
 table,
 formula
 )

 Runs formula for each row; returns table of results

Examples:
 // Calculate doubled prices
 ForAll(Products, Price * 2)
 
 // Add records with side effects
 ForAll(
 colNewOrders,
 Patch(Orders, Defaults(Orders), {
 ProductID: ProductID,
 Quantity: Quantity,
 OrderDate: Today()
 })
 )

 // Side effects: ForAll iterates and runs Patch each time

Notify per row:
 ForAll(colErrors, Notify("Error: " & ErrorMsg, NotificationType.Error))

Sequence (range):
 Sequence(5) → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
 Sequence(5, 10) → [10, 11, 12, 13, 14]
 
 ForAll(Sequence(10), ThisRecord.Value * 2) → [2, 4, 6, ..., 20]

Do-while equivalent:
 No native; use With and recursion is limited
 For repeated ops, use the data source's native filtering

The With function

With(record, formula)

Creates local scope for cleaner formulas

Without With:
 Sum(
 Filter(Sales, Region = ddlRegion.Selected.Value && Status = "Approved"),
 Amount
 ) - 
 Sum(
 Filter(Sales, Region = ddlRegion.Selected.Value && Status = "Refunded"),
 Amount
 )
 // Repeats the filter twice

With With:
 With(
 {filtered: Filter(Sales, Region = ddlRegion.Selected.Value)},
 Sum(Filter(filtered, Status = "Approved"), Amount) -
 Sum(Filter(filtered, Status = "Refunded"), Amount)
 )

Cleaner; more performant (filter once)

Common pattern:
 With(
 {user: User(), today: Today()},
 "Hello " & user.FullName & ", today is " & Text(today, "dddd")
 )

Worked example — form validation

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Registration form validation
// Form with: Name, Email, Age, Password, Confirm Password

// Validation messages

// lblNameError.Text:
If(
 IsBlank(txtName.Text),
 "Name is required",
 Len(txtName.Text) < 2,
 "Name must be at least 2 characters",
 ""
)

// lblEmailError.Text:
If(
 IsBlank(txtEmail.Text),
 "Email is required",
 !IsMatch(txtEmail.Text, Email),
 "Invalid email format",
 ""
)

// lblAgeError.Text:
If(
 IsBlank(txtAge.Text),
 "Age is required",
 !IsNumeric(txtAge.Text),
 "Age must be a number",
 Value(txtAge.Text) < 18,
 "Must be 18 or older",
 Value(txtAge.Text) > 120,
 "Invalid age",
 ""
)

// lblPasswordError.Text:
If(
 IsBlank(txtPassword.Text),
 "Password is required",
 Len(txtPassword.Text) < 8,
 "Password must be at least 8 characters",
 !IsMatch(txtPassword.Text, "[A-Z]"),
 "Password must contain uppercase",
 !IsMatch(txtPassword.Text, "[0-9]"),
 "Password must contain a number",
 ""
)

// lblConfirmError.Text:
If(
 txtConfirm.Text <> txtPassword.Text,
 "Passwords don't match",
 ""
)

// btnSubmit.DisplayMode:
With(
 {
 nameValid: !IsBlank(txtName.Text) && Len(txtName.Text) >= 2,
 emailValid: IsMatch(txtEmail.Text, Email),
 ageValid: IsNumeric(txtAge.Text) && Value(txtAge.Text) >= 18,
 passwordValid: Len(txtPassword.Text) >= 8 
 && IsMatch(txtPassword.Text, "[A-Z]")
 && IsMatch(txtPassword.Text, "[0-9]"),
 confirmValid: txtConfirm.Text = txtPassword.Text
 },
 If(
 And(nameValid, emailValid, ageValid, passwordValid, confirmValid),
 DisplayMode.Edit,
 DisplayMode.Disabled
 )
)

// btnSubmit.OnSelect:
Patch(
 Users,
 Defaults(Users),
 {
 Name: txtName.Text,
 Email: txtEmail.Text,
 Age: Value(txtAge.Text),
 PasswordHash: HashPassword(txtPassword.Text)
 }
);
Notify("Account created!", NotificationType.Success);
Navigate(scrLogin)

Common conditionals mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. = for assignment — that's comparison only; use Set/UpdateContext
  2. Comparing to Blank() with = — use IsBlank()
  3. Case-sensitive comparison — Power Fx string = is case-sensitive
  4. Nested If when Switch is cleaner — use Switch for value mapping
  5. Missing default in If — when none match, returns Blank()
  6. Boolean operator confusion — && is shorthand for And; || for Or; ! for Not
  7. IsBlank on 0 — 0 is not blank; check explicitly
  8. And/Or with non-boolean args — returns unexpected truthy results
  9. Switch missing default — when no case matches, returns Blank()
  10. Repeating same complex expression instead of using With
★ ON THE EXAM

"Conditional?" → If(condition, true, false).

"Multi-branch?" → If(c1, v1, c2, v2, ..., default) or Switch.

"Value comparison?" → Switch(expression, val1, result1, val2, result2, default).

"All conditions true?" → And(c1, c2, ...) or && operator.

"Any condition true?" → Or(c1, c2, ...) or || operator.

"Negate?" → Not(condition) or !.

"Test for null?" → IsBlank(value).

"Test for empty table?" → IsEmpty(table).

"Test for number?" → IsNumeric(value).

"Pattern match?" → IsMatch(text, pattern) — built-in Match constants.

"First non-blank?" → Coalesce(a, b, c, ...).

"Loop?" → ForAll(table, formula).

"Generate range?" → Sequence(n) or Sequence(n, start).

"Local scope for cleaner formula?" → With({var: value}, formula).

"Email validation?" → IsMatch(text, Email).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • If(condition, true, false) handles two-branch conditionals
  • If with multiple conditions: If(c1, v1, c2, v2, ..., default) — cascading evaluation
  • Switch is cleaner when comparing one value against many options
  • And, Or, Not for boolean composition; &&, ||, ! shorthand operators
  • Comparison operators: =, <>, <, >, <=, >=
  • String comparison is case-sensitive
  • IsBlank tests for null/empty; IsEmpty for tables with no rows
  • IsNumeric tests if value is a number (or numeric string)
  • IsMatch tests text against regex patterns; built-in Match constants (Email, Phone, etc.)
  • Coalesce returns the first non-blank value (fallback chain)
  • Conditional formatting: control properties like Visible, Color, DisplayMode use If/Switch
  • Validation patterns combine IsBlank, IsMatch, range checks with And
  • ForAll iterates a table; common for batch operations and side effects
  • Sequence(N) generates a numeric range for iteration
  • With({var: value}, formula) creates a local scope for cleaner, faster formulas

Comparison scope: the operators >, <, >=, <=, =, <> work on numbers, dates, AND strings — dates compare chronologically, strings alphabetically.

Connectors are how Power Apps talks to external services — Microsoft 365, SQL, Salesforce, custom APIs. Knowing standard vs premium tiers, common connectors, and limitations is essential. The PL-100 exam tests connector tiers and choosing the right one.

What connectors are

A connector = pre-built bridge between Power Apps and a service

Provides:
 - Authentication (handles OAuth, API keys)
 - Operations (Get records, Create, Update, Delete, etc.)
 - Schema (knows the structure of data)
 - Triggers (for Power Automate flows)
 - Rate limits and throttling

Without connectors:
 Would need to write API code from scratch
 Manage auth tokens, errors, retries manually

With connectors:
 Drag-and-drop integration
 Power Apps handles auth flow
 Use service's data as if local

Microsoft and partners build connectors:
 ~1000+ connectors available
 Microsoft 365, Azure, Dataverse, SQL Server
 Third-party: Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP, GitHub, etc.

Standard vs Premium connectors

StandardPremium
Included in Microsoft 365 licenseRequires Power Apps Premium license
Microsoft 365 servicesExternal enterprise services
Office 365 Users, SharePoint, OneDrive, OutlookSQL Server, Salesforce, Dataverse, on-prem
Free with Microsoft 365 planPer-app or per-user Power Apps plan

Standard connectors (Microsoft 365 included)

SharePoint
 - Lists, libraries, files
 - Common for simple data storage

OneDrive for Business / OneDrive (personal)
 - Excel files (cells, tables)
 - Document storage

Office 365 Users
 - Get manager, profile, photo
 - Look up users by email/ID

Office 365 Outlook
 - Read emails, send emails
 - Calendar events
 - Contacts

Office 365 Groups
 - Team membership operations
 - Group settings

Microsoft Teams
 - Channels, messages
 - Team operations

Excel Online (Business)
 - Read/write Excel files in OneDrive/SharePoint
 - Tables specifically

Planner
 - Tasks, plans, buckets

OneNote (Business)
 - Pages, sections

These are all FREE with most Microsoft 365 subscriptions

Premium connectors (Power Apps Premium)

Microsoft Dataverse
 - Premium data platform; relational, secure, scalable
 - The "preferred" data store for enterprise apps
 - Required for Model-Driven Apps

SQL Server (on-premises)
 - Connect via on-premises gateway
 - Stored procedures supported

SQL Server (Azure)
 - Direct cloud connection
 - No gateway needed

Salesforce
 - Read/write Salesforce data
 - OAuth authentication

Adobe Sign, DocuSign
 - eSignature workflows

SAP, Oracle, ServiceNow, GitHub
 - Enterprise integration

Common Data Service (older name for Dataverse)
 - Now called Dataverse

Premium requires:
 Each user of the app must have a Power Apps Premium license
 Per-app plans for specific apps
 Per-user plans for users with multiple apps

Custom connectors

When no built-in connector exists for a service:
 Create a Custom Connector

Setup:
 Power Apps maker portal → Data → Custom Connectors
 Or via Power Automate (same connector available in both)

Configure:
 General: name, description, icon
 Security: auth type (None, Basic, OAuth 2.0, API Key)
 Definition: URL, paths, parameters
 Definition (advanced): import OpenAPI spec, Postman collection
 Test: try operations live

Operations:
 Define each API endpoint
 HTTP verb (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
 Request URL and body
 Response schema (auto-generated from sample)

Sharing:
 Within environment
 Submit for certification to share globally (rare)

Use case: connect to internal REST APIs not covered by built-in connectors

Connection records

A "connection" is an instance of a connector with specific credentials

Visible in:
 make.powerapps.com → Connections (left nav)

Per user:
 Each user creates their own connections
 Authenticates with their account
 Sees only their connections (not others')

App connections:
 When you add a connector to an app, Power Apps prompts for connection
 Picks an existing one OR creates a new one
 Stored as part of the app

Sharing apps:
 When you share an app, users see "Connection needs login"
 They authenticate with their own account
 Their connection is then used for that app

Service principal:
 Enterprise alternative: use a single service account
 More complex setup; useful for shared apps

Common connector operations

Each connector exposes operations specific to its service

Common pattern:
 Get records (list / search / filter)
 Get single record (by ID)
 Create record
 Update record
 Delete record
 Subscribe to events (triggers, mostly for Power Automate)

Microsoft 365 examples:
 SharePoint:
 Get Items (filter, sort, paginate)
 Get Item (by ID)
 Create Item
 Update Item
 Delete Item
 
 Office 365 Outlook:
 Send Email (V2)
 Get Emails
 Forward Email
 Reply
 Mark as Read
 
 Office 365 Users:
 Get my profile (V2)
 Get user (V2)
 Get user photo
 Search for users (V2)

In Power Apps (canvas):
 Functions on connector mirror the operations:
 Office365Outlook.SendEmailV2("to", "subject", "body")
 SharePointConnector.GetItems("ListName")
 
 More typical: add as data source, use as table

Connector tier and licensing decision tree

Building an app for organizational use?

If data is in:
 SharePoint / Excel / OneDrive → Standard (free)
 Outlook / Calendar / Teams → Standard (free)
 Custom internal API (no service-specific connector) → Custom (free)

If data is in:
 Dataverse → Premium (Power Apps license required)
 SQL Server / Azure SQL → Premium
 Salesforce / SAP / Dynamics 365 → Premium
 Third-party SaaS → Premium

Mixed:
 If you use ANY premium connector → the WHOLE app requires premium license
 Workaround: split into separate apps (some standard, some premium)

Cost implications:
 Standard apps: covered by M365 subscription
 Premium apps: $5/user/app or $20/user (Power Apps per User)

Connector limits and throttling

Each connector has rate limits

Power Platform throttling:
 Per connection: typically 500-2000 requests/minute
 Per app: depends on license tier

Common limits:
 SharePoint: 600 requests/minute per user (Microsoft 365)
 Dataverse: high (designed for scale)
 Custom: varies by API source

Symptoms of throttling:
 HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests)
 App becomes slow or errors out

Mitigations:
 Use collections to cache data
 Batch operations where possible
 ForAll(Concurrent: true) for parallel ops
 Premium licenses allow higher limits

Delegation limits (separate; covered in next section):
 Power Apps may only return first N records (500 default)
 Some operations don't "delegate" to the source
 Affects what Filter/Sort/etc. can return

Delegation — the key constraint

DELEGATION
When you call Filter(BigTable, Status = "Active"):

Delegation works: Power Apps sends the filter to the data source. Server returns only matching rows. Fast, scalable.

Delegation fails: Power Apps pulls down up to 500 rows, then filters locally. If you have 10,000 rows, you'd miss 9,500.

Power Apps shows a blue underline / warning when an operation can't be delegated. 
Functions that DELEGATE in most sources:
 Filter with simple conditions (column = value)
 LookUp
 Sort, SortByColumns
 Count

Functions that often DON'T delegate:
 Search (text in any column)
 CountIf
 Complex conditions (combining multiple fields with calculations)
 String functions inside filters (Substitute, etc.)

Result row limits:
 Default: 500 rows
 Configurable: File → Settings → Advanced settings → Data row limit
 Maximum: 2000 (for some sources)

If query exceeds limit:
 Power Apps returns partial data without error
 Common cause of "missing data" bugs

Best practice:
 Watch for blue underline warnings
 Move complex logic to the source (views, stored procs in SQL)
 Use Dataverse for large datasets (good delegation support)

Common connector mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Using premium without realizing license cost — app silently requires premium for all users
  2. Confusing connector with connection — connector is the type; connection is an instance with creds
  3. Ignoring delegation warnings — blue underline means partial data
  4. Filter row limit forgotten — 500 default; missing records bug
  5. Connection sharing — each user has their own; auth on first launch
  6. Custom connector for simple thing — check standard connectors first
  7. Mixing connectors with no awareness — premium contagion across whole app
  8. Excel files not in OneDrive/SharePoint — only those locations are connectable
  9. SharePoint list with too many columns — slow operations
  10. Custom connector without proper auth setup — API calls fail
★ ON THE EXAM

"Connector tiers?" → Standard (Microsoft 365 included) and Premium (extra license).

"Standard examples?" → SharePoint, Excel, Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, Office 365 Users.

"Premium examples?" → Dataverse, SQL Server, Salesforce, SAP.

"Custom connector?" → Build your own for unsupported APIs.

"On-prem connection?" → On-premises Data Gateway required.

"Per-app vs per-user license?" → Per-app: $5/app/user; Per-user: $20/user (multiple apps).

"How are connectors authenticated?" → Each user creates their own connection.

"Delegation?" → Filter operations sent to source vs done locally with 500-row limit.

"Delegation warning?" → Blue underline in formula.

"Default row limit?" → 500; max 2000.

"When does an app become Premium?" → If ANY premium connector is used.

"Where to find connections?" → make.powerapps.com → Connections.

"Throttling response?" → HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Connectors are pre-built bridges to external services — handle auth, schema, operations
  • Two tiers: Standard (free with Microsoft 365) and Premium (extra Power Apps license)
  • Standard connectors: SharePoint, OneDrive, Outlook, Teams, Excel Online, Office 365 Users
  • Premium connectors: Dataverse, SQL Server, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, third-party SaaS
  • Custom connectors integrate APIs not covered by built-in (OpenAPI / Postman import)
  • Using ANY premium connector requires premium license for ALL users of the app
  • Connections are per-user instances of connectors with their credentials
  • Delegation: Power Apps sends operations to source if supported; falls back to 500-row limit if not
  • Watch for blue underline warnings indicating non-delegable operations
  • Default row limit is 500; configurable up to 2000 (File → Settings → Data row limit)
  • On-premises SQL needs the On-premises Data Gateway
  • Common operations: Get records, Create, Update, Delete, Search
  • Microsoft 365 connectors are FREE with M365 license
  • Rate limiting: 600 SharePoint req/min/user typical; HTTP 429 on throttle
  • Choose source based on data location, delegation needs, and license budget

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Dataverse is Microsoft's premium data platform — relational, secure, scalable, with rich features for business apps. It's the recommended backend for serious Power Apps work, and required for Model-Driven Apps. The PL-100 exam tests Dataverse concepts.

What Dataverse is

Dataverse = Microsoft's cloud-hosted relational database for business apps

History:
 Previously called "Common Data Service" (CDS)
 Renamed to "Microsoft Dataverse" in 2020

Key features:
 - Relational tables (rows and columns)
 - Built-in security (row-level, column-level)
 - Auditing and change tracking
 - Workflows and business rules
 - APIs (OData / REST)
 - Power Apps integration native
 - Dataverse for Teams (free tier, per-Team scope)

Use cases:
 - Power Apps backend
 - Power Automate workflow data store
 - Dynamics 365 (which is built on Dataverse)
 - Custom business apps

License:
 Premium feature in Power Apps
 Dataverse for Teams is free (limited)
 Dataverse for Dynamics 365 customers included

Dataverse vs SharePoint / SQL

FeatureDataverseSharePoint ListSQL Server
LicensePremiumStandard (M365)Premium
Row countMillions~30K usableMillions+
SecurityField-level + role-basedList-level / item-levelCustom; DB roles
RelationshipsNative; richLookup columns onlyFK constraints
DelegationExcellentGoodExcellent
WorkflowBuilt-in business rulesLimitedTriggers + procedures
AuditNativeVersion historyCustom
Best forEnterprise appsSmall lists, simple appsExisting SQL systems

Tables in Dataverse

A Dataverse table = relational table with rows and columns

Types:
 Standard tables:
 Built-in (Account, Contact, User, etc.)
 Designed for Dynamics 365 + Dataverse
 Pre-defined columns, relationships, business logic

 Custom tables:
 You create them
 Define your own columns
 Add relationships
 Suit your specific app needs

 Activity tables:
 Special type for time-stamped events
 Examples: Phone Call, Task, Email, Appointment
 Pre-built workflows and views

 Virtual tables:
 Data lives elsewhere (e.g., SQL, SAP)
 Dataverse provides a virtual interface
 Read/write through Dataverse but storage external

Naming:
 Display name: "Customer Account"
 Logical name (schema): "myorg_customeraccount" (lowercased; prefixed)
 Plural form: "Customer Accounts"

Adding a table:
 make.powerapps.com → Dataverse → Tables → + New

Columns (fields)

Each table has columns; many data types available

Data types:
 Single Line of Text — short string
 Multiline Text — long text
 Number (Whole, Decimal, Currency)
 Date and Time / Date Only
 Boolean (Yes/No)
 Choice — picklist with predefined options
 Choices (multi-select)
 Lookup — reference to another table's row
 File / Image
 Email — text with email validation
 Phone — text with phone validation
 URL — text with URL validation
 Owner — user/team reference
 Status — state machine (Active/Inactive)
 Status Reason — sub-status reason

Each column has:
 Display name + logical name
 Required (Required / Optional / Recommended)
 Searchable
 Audited (track changes)
 Calculated / Rollup (computed)
 Description (documentation)

Required columns:
 Display name (shown in UI)
 Logical name (used in formulas; usually auto-generated with prefix)
 Type (and type-specific options)

Primary name column

Every table has a "primary name column"
 Required when creating a table
 Used in lookup dropdowns (the display value)
 Default: "Name" but customizable

Examples:
 Customer Account → primary name = "Account Name"
 Contact → primary name = "Full Name"
 Order → primary name = "Order Number"

Choice carefully:
 Should be the field users see when picking from a list
 Often a meaningful string (not an ID)

In formulas:
 thisAccount.Name — primary name (or whatever you named it)

Relationships

Tables can reference each other via relationships

Three types:

ONE-TO-MANY (1:N):
 One Customer → Many Orders
 Customer has a "Orders" related list
 Order has a "Customer" lookup column
 Most common type

MANY-TO-ONE (N:1):
 Same as 1:N from the other side
 e.g., from Order's perspective: many Orders to one Customer

MANY-TO-MANY (N:N):
 Customer can have many Tags; Tag can apply to many Customers
 Junction table created automatically
 No direct foreign key; uses intermediate table

Create:
 Table → Relationships → + New
 Specify related table, type, and properties

Lookup column:
 Adding a lookup automatically creates a 1:N relationship
 Customer.OrdersLookup → references Account table

Cascade behavior:
 When parent (1 side) is deleted:
 Cascade Delete — children also deleted
 Restrict — block deletion if children exist
 Remove Link — children's lookup field cleared

Choices (option sets)

Choice = predefined picklist for a column

Example:
 Status column:
 Active (1)
 Inactive (2)
 Pending (3)

Defined at the table level (Local Choice) OR
 Reusable across tables (Global Choice)

Choice column types:
 Choice (single select)
 Choices (multi-select)
 Status (state with reason)

In Power Fx:
 Switch(Status.Value, "Active", ..., "Inactive", ...)
 
 Use .Value to compare string value
 .Label.Value for the label text

 ddlStatus.Items: Choices(Account.Status)
 // Returns the list of options for Account's Status column

Common confusion:
 Choice column = OptionSet in legacy terminology
 Status column = Status field in legacy
 Both serve similar purpose

Views

A view = saved query on a table

Like SQL view or SharePoint list view:
 Defines columns to show
 Filter conditions
 Sort order

Types of views:
 System views (built-in; everyone sees same)
 Personal views (per-user; user creates)

Examples:
 "Active Accounts" (filter: Status = Active)
 "My Open Tasks" (filter: Owner = currentUser, Status = Open)
 "All Customers" (no filter)

In Power Apps:
 Use views as data source filtering
 Gallery.Items = Accounts (defaults to all)
 Or: Filter(Accounts, view criteria) manually

Views are most useful in:
 Model-Driven Apps (built around them)
 Canvas apps via Filter() function

Business rules

No-code declarative logic for tables

Define conditions and actions:
 IF Status = "Closed" THEN
 Lock CloseDate column
 Lock Amount column
 
 IF Type = "Premium" THEN
 Make TotalRevenue column required
 Show ExtraField

Apply at:
 Form level (specific Model-Driven Apps form)
 Table level (everywhere)

Actions available:
 Set field value
 Set business required (Required / Optional / Recommended)
 Set visibility
 Lock/Unlock field
 Show error message
 Recommend a value
 Clear field value

Trigger:
 On form load
 On column value change

Business rules execute in Dataverse and in Model-Driven Apps
Canvas apps see the field changes but don't run the rules natively

Security model

Dataverse has rich security; far beyond SharePoint

Security roles:
 Each user has one or more roles
 Roles define WHO can do WHAT

Permissions per table:
 Create, Read, Write, Delete
 Append (link records to others)
 Append To (be linked from others)
 Assign (transfer ownership)
 Share

Scopes (who you can affect):
 None
 User (only your own records)
 Business Unit (records in your BU)
 Parent: Child BU (your BU and child BUs)
 Organization (all records)

Field-level security:
 Restrict access to specific columns
 Example: Salary field — only HR role can see

Hierarchy security:
 Manager can see direct reports' data
 Defined by hierarchical structure

Auditing:
 Track who changed what when
 Granular per table

Power Apps with Dataverse

In canvas app:
 Data → Add data → Search "Dataverse"
 Pick tables from your environment
 Use like any data source

Operations same as other connectors:
 Filter(Accounts, AccountType = "Premium")
 LookUp(Customers, ID = "C001", Name)
 Patch(Accounts, Defaults(Accounts), {Name: "ACME Corp"})
 Remove(Tasks, oldTask)

Dataverse advantages:
 Better delegation (more functions delegate vs SharePoint)
 Relationships traverse natively in formulas:
 LookUp(Orders, OrderID = "X").Customer.Name
 Native Image / File columns
 Native multi-select
 Better performance at scale

Model-Driven Apps:
 Use Dataverse natively
 Forms, views, business rules pre-built
 Minimum custom design needed

Dataverse for Teams (free tier)

Microsoft offers a free, scoped version of Dataverse for Teams

What's included:
 - Dataverse database within Microsoft Teams
 - One per team
 - Up to 2 GB capacity, 1 million rows per table
 - Build Power Apps and Automate flows in Teams
 - No premium license needed for users of the app within Teams

Limitations:
 - Scoped to the Team (not shared across orgs)
 - Limited capacity
 - Some features missing (no service principal, fewer security options)
 - Apps run only in Teams (not standalone)

Use case:
 - Small team apps
 - Quick prototypes
 - Build → publish to Teams channel → use immediately

Upgrade path:
 Move to full Dataverse environment for larger scale

Common Dataverse mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Confusing CDS and Dataverse — same thing, renamed
  2. Using SharePoint when Dataverse is right — for >30K rows or enterprise data
  3. Forgetting Dataverse is Premium — license cost
  4. Lookup column data types confusion — store actual record, not just ID
  5. Choice value vs label — use .Value for code; .Label.Value for display
  6. Ignoring business rules when they'd reduce form code
  7. Missing primary name column on table creation
  8. Cascade delete unconfigured — orphan records or unwanted deletions
  9. Wrong security scope — user sees too much or too little
  10. Using full Dataverse when Dataverse for Teams suffices — pay for unneeded
★ ON THE EXAM

"Premium data platform?" → Dataverse.

"Old name?" → Common Data Service (CDS).

"Required for what?" → Model-Driven Apps; also recommended for enterprise canvas apps.

"Free tier?" → Dataverse for Teams (per-team scope).

"Tables vs columns?" → Tables hold rows; columns are the fields.

"Relationship types?" → 1:N (one-to-many), N:1 (many-to-one), N:N (many-to-many).

"Linking tables?" → Lookup column creates a 1:N relationship.

"Predefined picklist?" → Choice column (option set in legacy).

"Saved queries?" → Views (system or personal).

"No-code logic on forms?" → Business rules.

"Restrict field access?" → Field-level security.

"Permissions per user?" → Security roles.

"Delete parent + children?" → Cascade Delete.

"Block delete if children?" → Restrict.

"Primary name column?" → Required; the display name shown in lookups.

"Power Apps function for choices?" → Choices(Table.ColumnName) returns the list.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Dataverse (formerly CDS) is Microsoft's premium relational database for business apps
  • Required for Model-Driven Apps; recommended for serious canvas apps at scale
  • Premium feature; Dataverse for Teams is a free scoped alternative
  • Tables are relational; columns have rich data types (text, number, date, choice, lookup, etc.)
  • Relationships: 1:N, N:1, N:N — automatic junction table for N:N
  • Lookup columns automatically create 1:N relationships
  • Primary name column is the "display name" used in lookups (required at creation)
  • Choices = predefined picklists; access via Choices(Table.Column) in Power Fx
  • Views are saved queries (system or personal); foundational in Model-Driven Apps
  • Business rules = declarative form logic (show/hide, required, set value)
  • Security: roles with permissions per table; scopes (User/BU/Org); field-level security
  • Cascade behaviors: Delete, Restrict, Remove Link — define on relationships
  • Delegation is excellent — most operations push to Dataverse
  • In canvas apps, Dataverse used like any data source via Add Data
  • Audit and change tracking are built-in (vs SharePoint version history)
  • Compared to SharePoint: more scalable, more relational, more secure, more expensive

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Modeling data correctly — choosing right column types, defining relationships properly, planning for delegation — separates an app that scales from one that breaks. The PL-100 exam tests creating tables, choosing column types, and configuring relationships.

Creating a custom table

make.powerapps.com → Dataverse → Tables → + New table

Configuration:
 Display name: "Project" (singular)
 Plural display name: "Projects"
 Schema name: auto-generated (yourprefix_project)
 Primary name column: "Project Name" (default; rename if needed)
 Description: documentation
 
Advanced options:
 Owner type: User or Team (typical) vs Organization
 Enable for:
 Activities — can have related activities (tasks, emails, etc.)
 Notes — can have attached notes
 Auditing — track changes
 Mobile — visible in mobile apps
 Touch-friendly — optimized UI
 Quick Create — fast inline form
 Duplicate Detection — alert on duplicates
 Allow Bulk Edit, Allow Bulk Delete
 
Save:
 Creates table with primary name column already in place
 Add more columns next

Adding columns

Inside a table → Columns → + Add column

For each column:
 Display name
 Type (see below)
 Type-specific settings (max length, decimal places, etc.)
 Required (Optional / Recommended / Required)
 Searchable
 Auditing
 Advanced: description, default value

Schema name auto-generated:
 yourprefix_columnname
 Lowercase with prefix
 Used in formulas (Power Fx normalizes display name → schema)

Common column setup examples:

 Start Date (Date Only)
 Required: Optional
 Default: Today()
 
 Status (Choice)
 Required: Required
 Options: Active, On Hold, Completed
 Default: Active
 
 Manager (Lookup → User)
 Required: Recommended
 Target table: User (or Contact)
 
 Description (Text → Multiline)
 Max length: 4000
 Searchable: Yes
 
 Budget (Currency)
 Decimals: 2
 Min: 0
 Max: 10,000,000

Data types in depth

Text:
 Single line of text (default; max 4000 chars)
 Multiline text (long; max ~1 MB)
 Email (validates format)
 Phone (validates format)
 URL (renders as link)
 Ticker (stock) (specific format)
 Text Area (multi-line short)

Number:
 Whole Number (integers; -2.1B to +2.1B)
 Decimal (high precision; 10 places)
 Floating Point (less precision; faster)
 Currency (with currency code; auto-conversion)

Date/Time:
 Date and Time (full timestamp)
 Date Only (no time)
 Time-zone behavior:
 User local (display per user's TZ)
 Time-zone independent (same time everywhere)

Boolean (Yes/No):
 Display Yes/No, On/Off, True/False, Allow/Don't Allow, etc.

Choice:
 Single-select with predefined options
 Local (per table) or Global (reusable)
 Each option has Label + Value (integer)

Choices (multi-select):
 Like Choice but multiple values

Lookup:
 Reference to another table's row
 Stores reference + display value of related row

Status / Status Reason:
 State machine pattern
 Status: Active / Inactive
 Status Reason: sub-reason within state

Owner:
 Special lookup to User or Team
 Used for security and assignments

Customer:
 Special lookup that can point to either Account or Contact

Calculated and rollup columns

Calculated column:
 Computed on the fly (no stored value)
 Reactive to changes in source columns
 
 Example:
 "FullName" = FirstName + " " + LastName
 "DiscountedPrice" = Price * 0.9
 
 Limitations:
 Some functions not allowed (cross-table, aggregations)
 Performance: don't put complex calcs in views with many rows

Rollup column:
 Aggregation across related records
 Updated periodically (not real-time)
 
 Example on Customer table:
 "TotalRevenue" = SUM of Orders.Amount where Status = "Closed"
 
 Recalculation:
 Every hour by default
 Or on-demand via UI button
 Not as live as calculated columns

Use cases:
 Calc: same-row derived values
 Rollup: cross-record aggregations

1:N relationships in detail

Most common; one parent, many children

Example:
 Parent: Customer (1)
 Child: Order (N)
 Each Order has ONE Customer
 Each Customer has MANY Orders

Create:
 Option 1: Add a Lookup column on the child table
 Order table → + Add column → Lookup → Customer
 Automatically creates 1:N relationship
 
 Option 2: Explicitly via Relationships tab
 Customer table → Relationships → + New (1:N type)
 Specify child table (Order) and behavior

After creation:
 Customer page shows "Related → Orders" tab
 Order has a "Customer" lookup column

Cascade behaviors (configurable):
 Assign:
 When parent is reassigned, reassign children?
 Options: Cascade All / Cascade Active / Cascade User-Owned / Cascade None
 
 Delete:
 When parent is deleted, what happens?
 Cascade Delete — children deleted too
 Restrict — block parent delete if children exist
 Remove Link — clear children's lookup field
 Restrict — recommended for safety
 
 Reparent / Share / Unshare:
 Similar options for ownership and sharing

N:N relationships

Many-to-many: each side can have multiple of the other

Example:
 Customer ↔ Tag
 Customer "ACME" has Tags: VIP, Tech, Eastern
 Tag "VIP" applies to Customers: ACME, Globex, Initech

Create:
 Customer table → Relationships → + New (N:N type)
 Specify other table (Tag)
 Dataverse creates a hidden junction table

Junction table:
 Stores pairs of (CustomerID, TagID)
 Not directly visible in maker portal
 Power Apps handles linking through the relationship

In canvas apps:
 Add Tag to Customer:
 Relate(thisCustomer.Tags, thisTag)
 
 Remove Tag from Customer:
 Unrelate(thisCustomer.Tags, thisTag)
 
 Get all Tags for a Customer:
 ForAll(thisCustomer.Tags, ...)

In Model-Driven Apps:
 Subgrid on Customer form shows related Tags
 Built-in "Add existing" and "Add new" buttons

Polymorphic lookups

A lookup that can reference different tables

Special types in Dataverse:
 Customer = can be Account OR Contact
 Regarding = can be many activity-related tables
 Owner = User OR Team

Custom polymorphic lookups (advanced):
 Less common; complex setup
 Power Apps formulas need to check target type

In formulas:
 thisRecord.Customer.Name — Power Fx auto-resolves to either Account.Name or Contact.FullName

Use sparingly:
 Adds complexity
 Standard 1:N usually cleaner

Worked example — project tracking schema

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Project management tables
// Schema for a project tracking app

// Table: Project
// Columns:
// Name (primary; text, required)
// Description (multiline, optional)
// StartDate (date only, required)
// EndDate (date only, optional)
// Status (choice: Planning/Active/On Hold/Completed/Cancelled)
// Budget (currency, optional)
// Owner (owner lookup → User, required)
// CompletionPct (whole number 0-100, default 0)

// Table: Task
// Columns:
// Title (primary; text, required)
// Description (multiline)
// DueDate (date only)
// Status (choice: To Do / In Progress / Done)
// Priority (choice: Low / Medium / High / Critical)
// AssignedTo (lookup → User)
// Project (lookup → Project, required) ← creates 1:N
// EstimatedHours (decimal)
// ActualHours (decimal)

// Table: Tag (for categorizing projects)
// Columns:
// Name (primary; text, required)
// Color (text)

// Relationships:
// Project (1) → Task (N) via Task.Project lookup
// Project (N) ↔ Tag (N) via N:N relationship
// Task.AssignedTo → User (1:N from User to Task)

// Calculated column on Project:
// TaskCount = COUNT of related Tasks
// (or use Rollup: TotalEstimatedHours = SUM of Task.EstimatedHours)

// Rollup column on Project:
// TotalActualHours = SUM(Task.ActualHours) WHERE Task.Project = thisProject

// Business rule on Task:
// IF Status = "Done" THEN Set ActualHours required = true
// IF Priority = "Critical" THEN Show Owner-only color flag

// Cascade behaviors:
// Project → Task: Cascade Delete (deleting project removes tasks)
// Project → Tag: Remove Link (deleting project doesn't affect tags)
// Task → User: Restrict (don't delete users who have tasks)

Querying related records

Power Fx with Dataverse:

Get child records:
 Filter(Tasks, Project = thisProject)

 Or via the relationship navigation:
 thisProject.Tasks // returns table of related tasks

Get parent record:
 thisTask.Project // returns the parent Project record
 thisTask.Project.Name // its name

Navigate through chains:
 thisTask.AssignedTo.Manager.Email

 Works as long as relationships exist
 Each level is a Dataverse lookup
 Power Apps handles auto-fetching

Performance:
 Each navigation may trigger a query
 For lists, use AddColumns and explicit Filter for control
 Dataverse caches in app session

Common modeling mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Storing IDs as text instead of using Lookup columns — lose referential integrity
  2. One huge table instead of normalized — query inefficiency
  3. Missing primary name meaningful — bad lookup display
  4. Cascade Delete unchecked — orphan records on parent deletion
  5. Cascade Delete too aggressive — accidental mass deletions
  6. Choice vs Lookup confusion — Choice = static list; Lookup = reference to another table
  7. Calculated columns referencing cross-table — usually not allowed
  8. N:N when 1:N would suffice — over-engineered
  9. Forgetting required vs business required — business rules handle conditional required
  10. Schema name conflicts — same name from different solutions
★ ON THE EXAM

"Create custom table?" → make.powerapps.com → Dataverse → Tables → + New.

"Required at creation?" → Display name, primary name column, schema name (auto).

"Primary name column?" → Shown in lookups; used as default display.

"Column types?" → Text, Number, Date, Boolean, Choice, Lookup, Owner, etc.

"Computed column (same row)?" → Calculated column.

"Aggregation across related records?" → Rollup column (not real-time).

"Add a relationship?" → Lookup column (auto-creates 1:N) or Relationships tab.

"Many-to-many?" → N:N relationship with auto junction table.

"Add tag to record?" → Relate(parent.Tags, tag).

"Remove tag?" → Unrelate(parent.Tags, tag).

"Cascade behaviors?" → Cascade Delete / Restrict / Remove Link on relationships.

"Owner column?" → User or Team reference; security implications.

"Customer column?" → Polymorphic; Account OR Contact.

"Required levels?" → Optional / Recommended / Required.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Custom tables created via make.powerapps.com → Dataverse → Tables → + New
  • Every table has a primary name column (the display field for lookups)
  • Column types include text, number, date, boolean, choice, lookup, owner, customer
  • Choices = predefined picklists; can be local (per-table) or global (reusable)
  • Lookup columns reference rows in other tables; auto-create 1:N relationships
  • Calculated columns compute on the fly within the same row
  • Rollup columns aggregate across related rows; updated periodically (not real-time)
  • Relationship types: 1:N (one-to-many), N:1 (inverse), N:N (many-to-many with junction)
  • Add Lookup column = create 1:N relationship
  • N:N relationships use Relate / Unrelate functions in Power Fx
  • Cascade behaviors: Cascade Delete / Restrict / Remove Link on relationship config
  • Owner type = User or Team (typical); affects security and assignments
  • Polymorphic lookups (Customer, Owner, Regarding) reference multiple table types
  • Navigate relationships in formulas: thisRecord.RelatedField.AnotherField
  • Required levels: Optional, Recommended, Required (with red asterisk)
  • Plan schema carefully; restructuring after many records is painful

For free Microsoft 365-licensed apps, SharePoint Lists and Excel files are the two go-to backends. Knowing their capabilities, quirks, and limitations is essential. The PL-100 exam tests connecting to these and recognizing limitations like delegation.

SharePoint Lists as data source

SharePoint Lists are Microsoft's "lightweight database" included in M365

Strengths:
 - Free with Microsoft 365 license
 - Built-in versioning and approvals
 - Built-in permissions (per-item if needed)
 - Easy to set up (creator portal)
 - Good integration with Teams, Power Automate
 - Forms built-in (basic)

Limits:
 - Recommended ~30,000 items per list (5,000 view threshold)
 - Limited delegation (compared to Dataverse)
 - No true relationships (only lookup columns)
 - No proper transactions
 - Less performant than Dataverse at scale

Use when:
 - Small to medium data sets
 - Microsoft 365 only (no premium budget)
 - Quick prototyping
 - Team collaboration features needed

SharePoint list column types

TypeNotes
Single line of textMax 255 chars
Multiple linesLong text; can be Rich Text
NumberInteger or decimal
Date and TimeFull timestamp or date only
Yes/NoBoolean
ChoiceSingle or multi-select dropdown
Person or GroupUser reference; can multi-select
LookupReference to another list
CalculatedFormula referencing other columns
Hyperlink or pictureURL field
Managed MetadataTerm store-driven

Connecting SharePoint to Power Apps

In Power Apps Studio:
 Data tab → + Add data → Search "SharePoint"
 
Connection setup:
 Enter SharePoint site URL (e.g., https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Team)
 Or pick a recent site
 
Pick list(s):
 See all lists in the site
 Select one or many

Result:
 List appears in Data sources panel
 Usable as a table in formulas:
 Filter(Tasks, Status = "Open")
 Patch(Tasks, Defaults(Tasks), {...})
 Remove(Tasks, oldItem)

Form binding:
 Form.DataSource = Tasks // SharePoint list
 Form.Item = Gallery1.Selected

Custom views:
 SharePoint views accessible: list.Views
 Or filter manually with Power Fx

SharePoint Choice columns in Power Apps

Choice columns return RECORDS, not just strings

For single-select Choice:
 item.Status → record like {Value: "Open"}
 item.Status.Value → the string "Open"
 
 Compare:
 item.Status.Value = "Open" → boolean
 
 Set in Patch:
 Patch(Tasks, item, {Status: {Value: "Closed"}})
 // Must pass as record with Value field

For multi-select Choice:
 item.Categories → table of records (each has Value)
 Concat(item.Categories, Value, ", ") → "A, B, C"
 
 Set in Patch:
 Patch(Tasks, item, {Categories: [{Value:"A"}, {Value:"B"}]})

For Person field:
 item.Assignee → record
 item.Assignee.Email → email
 item.Assignee.DisplayName → name
 
 Single person:
 {DepartmentName: "", Claims: "i:0#.f|membership|" & userEmail, ...}
 
 Multi-person:
 Array of person records

SharePoint delegation

SharePoint has decent but limited delegation

DELEGABLE operations:
 Filter with simple conditions on indexed columns
 StartsWith
 Sort by indexed column
 LookUp

NOT DELEGABLE:
 CountIf (on most field types)
 Search across multiple columns
 String operations in filter (Substitute, etc.)
 Filtering by Choice column with complex formulas

Indexed columns:
 SharePoint allows indexing some columns (up to 20 per list)
 Indexed = faster, more likely to delegate
 Configure: List settings → Indexed columns

Common workaround:
 Pull subset locally with delegation-friendly filter
 Then refine locally
 
 E.g.:
 ClearCollect(colCache, Filter(Tasks, Status.Value = "Open"))
 Then use Search(colCache, ...) locally

Row limit:
 Default 500; configurable up to 2000 (File → Settings)
 Will silently truncate beyond limit

SharePoint advanced patterns

Lookups in SharePoint:
 Lookup column references another list
 In Power Apps:
 item.ParentList → record
 item.ParentList.Value → display value (column from parent)
 item.ParentList.Id → ID of parent record

Adding to a person column:
 Patch(Tasks, item, {Assignee: {
 DepartmentName: "",
 Claims: "i:0#.f|membership|alice@example.com",
 Department: "",
 DisplayName: "Alice",
 Email: "alice@example.com",
 JobTitle: "",
 Picture: ""
 }})

Versioning:
 Enable in list settings → Version history
 Power Apps automatically respects versioning
 Edit form shows current version
 Can roll back via SharePoint UI

Permissions:
 List-level or per-item
 Power Apps respects user's permissions
 User without permission sees empty or error

Attachments:
 Form's attachment control: AttachmentControl1.Attachments
 Files stored within the list item
 Native support in Edit/Display forms

Excel Online as data source

Excel files stored in OneDrive or SharePoint can serve as data source

Setup:
 Convert relevant data range to a Table (Ctrl+T in Excel)
 Save in OneDrive for Business or SharePoint
 In Power Apps: Data → + Add data → Excel Online (Business)
 Select file, then specific Table

What Power Apps sees:
 Each Excel Table = one data source (like a SharePoint list)
 Columns inferred from Excel headers
 Data types: text, number, date inferred from Excel

Limitations:
 - Severely limited delegation (almost everything pulls locally)
 - Default 500-row limit (max 2000)
 - No relationships
 - No proper concurrency control (last writer wins)
 - Slow for many users
 - File can get corrupted on heavy use

When to use Excel:
 - Small datasets (< 500 rows ideally)
 - Quick prototypes
 - Personal apps
 - Read-only reference data

When NOT to use:
 - Multi-user concurrent writes (data loss risk)
 - Larger data sets
 - Production apps that need to scale

Excel vs SharePoint vs Dataverse

CapabilityExcelSharePointDataverse
Row capacityTiny~30KMillions
DelegationPoorDecentExcellent
RelationshipsNoneLookups onlyNative 1:N, N:N
Concurrent usersRiskyOKExcellent
SecurityFile-levelItem-levelField-level
LicenseM365 (standard)M365 (standard)Premium
Best forPrototypesTeam appsEnterprise

Common SharePoint/Excel mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Excel for production multi-user app — data loss risk
  2. Patching Choice as string — must use {Value: "..."} record
  3. Forgetting Choices() for dropdowns — empty list shown
  4. Person field as text — needs full Claims record structure
  5. Default 500-row limit — silent truncation; raise to 2000 if needed
  6. Indexing not configured on filter columns → delegation fails
  7. Refresh forgotten — app shows stale data after edits elsewhere
  8. SharePoint Lookup vs Choice confusion — Lookup is reference, Choice is fixed options
  9. Date/time-zone issues — SharePoint stores UTC; display in user's TZ
  10. Mass operations exceeding limits — ForAll on big set hits throttling
★ ON THE EXAM

"Free data source with M365?" → SharePoint List or Excel Online.

"SharePoint row limit?" → ~30K usable; 5K view threshold.

"Choice column in Patch?" → {Value: "..."} record syntax.

"Dropdown from list field?" → Choices(ListName.ColumnName).

"Person field?" → Returns record with DisplayName, Email, Claims, etc.

"Re-fetch data?" → Refresh(DataSource).

"Delegation warning?" → Blue underline; non-delegable function or field.

"Default row limit?" → 500; max 2000.

"Excel as Power Apps source?" → Must be a Table (Ctrl+T) in OneDrive/SharePoint.

"Excel best use?" → Prototypes only; not production multi-user.

"Add SharePoint to app?" → Data → + Add data → SharePoint → Site → List.

"Person field multi-select?" → Returns table of person records.

"Filter for delegation?" → Use indexed columns and simple conditions.

"Attachments to list item?" → Native Attachments control on Edit form.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • SharePoint Lists and Excel Online are free Standard connectors with Microsoft 365
  • SharePoint: better for production; ~30K rows usable; built-in versioning and permissions
  • Excel: limited; prototypes only; no concurrency control; ~500 rows practical
  • SharePoint column types include Person/Group, Lookup, Choice, Yes/No, Calculated
  • In Power Apps, add via Data → + Add data → SharePoint or Excel Online (Business)
  • Excel files must be in OneDrive or SharePoint; data must be in a Table (Ctrl+T)
  • Choice columns return records with .Value (and .Label for SharePoint)
  • Patch a Choice: {Value: "Open"} — pass as record, not bare string
  • Dropdowns from a list's Choice column: Choices(ListName.ColumnName)
  • Person field returns a record with DisplayName, Email, Claims
  • SharePoint delegation: simple conditions, indexed columns; complex ops fall back locally
  • Default row limit 500; configurable up to 2000 (File → Settings)
  • Indexed SharePoint columns improve delegation/performance
  • Refresh(DataSource) re-fetches latest data into the app
  • Attachments: native control on Edit forms for SharePoint
  • For enterprise data needs, Dataverse is the recommended upgrade

Model-Driven Apps are the "data-first" counterpart to canvas apps. Instead of pixel-perfect design, you get a consistent UI auto-generated from your data model. They're the foundation of Dynamics 365 and major enterprise apps. The PL-100 exam tests model-driven app creation and navigation.

What model-driven apps are

Model-driven app = app where the DATA MODEL drives the UI

You don't drag-and-drop screens like canvas apps
Instead, you configure:
 - Tables (data model)
 - Forms (data entry/display)
 - Views (list/search)
 - Charts (analytics)
 - Business processes
 - Site map (navigation)

Power Apps auto-generates the consistent UI based on your config

Pros:
 - Fast to build (no pixel-pushing)
 - Consistent UI across all apps in environment
 - Built-in features: search, filter, export, audit, charts
 - Responsive (works on web, mobile, tablet)
 - Better for complex business processes

Cons:
 - Less visual customization
 - Looks "corporate" (rigid layout)
 - Requires Dataverse (premium license)
 - Steeper learning curve for makers used to canvas

Canvas vs Model-Driven comparison

Canvas AppsModel-Driven Apps
Design-first (pixel control)Data-first (model-driven)
Any data sourceRequires Dataverse
PowerPoint-likeOffice 365-like
Mobile-first designResponsive automatically
Custom layoutsConsistent layout
Per-screen logicBusiness rules + workflows
Standard license OKPremium license required
Best for: unique UXBest for: process-heavy data apps

Creating a model-driven app

make.powerapps.com → + Create → Model-driven app

Or via Solutions:
 Solutions → + New → Model-driven app

App designer:
 Name, description, icon
 Navigation: where in left menu
 Add pages (Dataverse tables)
 Configure components for each page

For each table page:
 Select forms to use
 Select views to use
 Charts to include
 Dashboards to feature

Save → Play to test

Site map (navigation):
 Tree of areas, groups, subareas
 Maps to left-nav menu
 Each subarea = a page (table or web resource)

Components of a model-driven app

Pages:
 Each entity (table) you want to include
 Shows views, forms, charts, related items

Forms:
 Main form (default editing view)
 Quick view form (mini info card; embedded in other forms)
 Quick create form (fast inline create)
 Card form (for grids)

Views:
 System views: Active, Inactive, All, etc.
 Custom views: filtered queries
 Hierarchical views (org charts)

Charts:
 Bar, column, line, pie, funnel
 Pre-built on views
 Real-time data

Dashboards:
 Combine multiple charts + views
 Personalized or system dashboards

Business processes:
 Visualized stages (Lead → Opportunity → Won/Lost)
 Stage gates and required fields

Workflows:
 Background automation (deprecated in favor of Power Automate)

The Maker Designer interface

Modern app designer (since 2021):
 Left: Pages tree
 Center: Configuration for selected page
 Right: Properties / Components

Add components to a page:
 Form (default: main form auto-selected)
 Views (default: system Active view selected)
 Charts
 Dashboards
 Web resources (custom HTML/JS)

Site map:
 Click "Edit" on Site map
 Drag areas, groups, subareas
 Each subarea links to a table page or URL

Settings:
 General settings
 Theme (color scheme)
 Mobile (allowed devices)

Test:
 Click Play to launch app
 Edit in separate tab

Site map / Navigation

Hierarchical menu structure:

 Area

 Area

Example for a Sales app:
 Sales Area
 Customers Group

 Contacts (subarea → Contact table)

Configure via site map designer:
 Drag-and-drop tree manipulation
 Set icons and labels
 Link each subarea to a content type

This becomes the left navigation in the runtime app

Pages and entity navigation

When user clicks "Accounts" in site map:
 Lands on Account list page
 Shows current view (e.g., "Active Accounts")

User selects an account row:
 Opens that record's main form
 Shows all fields, sub-grids of related records, tabs

Form is editable in-place:
 Click field, edit, click Save
 Quick save in header (without leaving form)

Related records:
 "Related" tab in form
 Shows children based on 1:N relationships
 Sub-grids for orders, tasks, etc.

Form behavior:
 Auto-save on field change (toggleable)
 Mandatory field warnings
 Business rules trigger live (validation, show/hide, etc.)

Theming and branding

Customization options:
 Theme: primary color, accent color, header style
 Logo: upload custom
 Background images

Configure:
 Settings → Themes
 Create new theme, define colors
 Apply to specific apps or environment-wide

Limitations:
 Less control than canvas apps
 Layout is rigid (form/view structure stays consistent)
 Best for "corporate" feel rather than unique branding

Mobile experience

Model-driven apps work natively on mobile:
 - Power Apps mobile app on iOS / Android
 - Auto-adapted layouts
 - Touch-optimized controls
 - Works offline (some features cached)

Power Apps mobile:
 Install on phone
 Sign in with M365 account
 Apps user has access to listed
 Tap to launch any model-driven (or canvas) app

Tablet support:
 Bigger screens optimize automatically
 More columns shown in views
 Form layouts adjust

Offline:
 Configurable per table
 Records cached locally
 Sync when connection restored

Sharing model-driven apps

Two parts:
 1. Share the app itself
 2. Grant Dataverse permissions

Share app:
 App designer → Share → add users
 Assign one or more security roles

Security roles:
 Required for model-driven apps
 Define permissions on tables (Create/Read/Write/Delete/Append/Assign/Share)
 Define scopes (User/BU/Org)
 
 Pre-built roles:
 System Administrator (full access)
 System Customizer (modify config)
 Salesperson (limited to own records)
 Custom roles (your own)

For each user:
 Grant security role assignment via admin center
 User gets access to app + can perform operations role allows

Common model-driven app mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Trying to pixel-design model-driven — that's canvas; MDA is config-driven
  2. No Dataverse environment — MDA requires Dataverse
  3. Forgetting security roles — users can't access without role
  4. Sharing app without table permissions — user sees app but no data
  5. Custom forms without testing all roles — different roles see different things
  6. Hardcoded views instead of system views
  7. Missing site map — users can't navigate
  8. Auto-save disabled — users lose work
  9. Business rules without testing — silent failures or unexpected behavior
  10. Form not published — changes don't appear
★ ON THE EXAM

"Data-first app type?" → Model-driven app.

"Required data store?" → Microsoft Dataverse (premium).

"Configure rather than design?" → MDA paradigm.

"App components?" → Pages (tables), Forms, Views, Charts, Dashboards, Business Processes.

"Navigation?" → Site map (Area → Group → Subarea).

"Page maps to?" → A table (entity) — shows its forms and views.

"Multiple forms per table?" → Main, Quick View, Quick Create, Card.

"Quick create form?" → Fast inline new record creation.

"Pre-built role?" → System Administrator, System Customizer, Salesperson, etc.

"Sharing requires?" → App share + security role assignment.

"Mobile experience?" → Power Apps mobile app; auto-responsive.

"Offline?" → Configurable per table; caches data, syncs when online.

"Where to create app?" → make.powerapps.com → + Create → Model-driven app.

"Business process flow?" → Visual stages with required fields per stage.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Model-driven apps are "data-first" — UI auto-generated from data model
  • Require Dataverse (premium license)
  • Configure tables, forms, views, charts, dashboards, site map
  • No pixel-design like canvas; consistent corporate look across all model-driven apps
  • Pages = tables added to the app; show forms, views, charts
  • Site map = hierarchical menu (Area → Group → Subarea) for navigation
  • Multiple form types per table: Main, Quick View, Quick Create, Card
  • Views = saved queries (system or personal) defining filter, columns, sort
  • Charts visualize views; pre-built types (bar, column, line, pie, funnel)
  • Dashboards combine multiple views and charts
  • Business processes provide guided stages with required fields per stage
  • Security roles required to access; pre-built roles or custom
  • Share app + grant security roles separately
  • Mobile native via Power Apps mobile app; offline cache supported
  • Best for: process-heavy data apps where consistency > uniqueness
  • Make modifications via Power Apps maker portal (no code in most cases)

Forms and views are the bread-and-butter of model-driven apps. Forms control how a single record is displayed and edited. Views control how lists of records are searched and presented. The PL-100 exam tests form types, view configuration, and customization.

Form types

Form TypePurpose
MainPrimary editing view; full-screen experience
Quick ViewMini info card embedded on another form to show related record info
Quick CreateLightweight form for fast inline record creation
CardCompact form for use in mobile/dashboard grids

Main form anatomy

A main form has three main areas:

Header (top):
 Primary name field large
 Quick info: status, owner, key metrics
 Save and other commands

Body:
 Tabs (horizontal sections)
 Each tab has Sections (vertical groupings)
 Sections contain Fields and Sub-grids
 
 Example tabs:
 Summary, Details, Activities, Related, History

Footer (bottom; optional):
 Less common; for additional commands or info

Form designer:
 Visual layout designer
 Drag fields, sub-grids, components into sections
 Configure properties of each component
 Preview as you build

Adding components to a form

Components panel (right side):

 Fields:
 Drag from "Fields" tab onto a section
 All table columns available
 Configure properties: required, read-only, visibility

 Sub-grids:
 Embedded list of related records
 Show 1:N related items inline (e.g., Tasks on Account form)
 Configure: which view to use, filter, default sort

 Quick view forms:
 Embed a Quick View form to show data from related record
 Example: Account's Primary Contact info on Account form

 Components (newer):
 Timeline (for activities)
 Form Component Control (reusable mini-form)
 Code components (PCF — Power Apps Component Framework)

 Tab sections:
 1-column section
 2-column section
 3-column section
 Reference panel (right-side panel)

Field-level configuration

For each field on a form:

 Required: Optional / Recommended / Required
 (Per-form override; field's underlying setting is default)
 
 Read-only:
 Field can be displayed but not edited on this form
 
 Visible:
 Hide field entirely
 Use business rules for conditional visibility
 
 Label:
 Override the column's display name on this specific form
 
 Lock the field:
 Prevent edits to specific form section by certain roles
 
 Show on phone:
 Toggle visibility on mobile devices

Multiple forms per table:
 Salespeople form vs Managers form
 Same table; different layouts
 Form security: role-based access

Quick view forms

Quick View = compact form embedded in another form
 Shows info about a related (looked-up) record

Use case:
 Account form has a "Primary Contact" lookup
 Quick View on Account shows Contact's phone, email, title
 No need to click into Contact record to see basic info

Setup:
 1. Create a Quick View form on the Contact table
 - Specify which fields to show
 2. On Account's main form, add Quick View
 3. Bind it to the Contact lookup
 4. Power Apps auto-renders contact info inline

Quick View form has:
 - Tabs and sections like main form
 - But typically smaller
 - Read-only (display only; no editing)

Multiple Quick Views possible:
 Account can have Quick View of Primary Contact, Owner, Manager, etc.

Quick Create forms

Quick Create = fast inline form for creating new records

Use case:
 Adding a new Contact while filling Account form
 Don't navigate to Contact list, just inline form pops up

Setup:
 Enable "Allow quick create" on the table
 Create a Quick Create form on that table
 Designate which fields appear (usually minimal: name, email, phone)

User experience:
 In a lookup field on a form, "+ New" appears
 Click → mini panel slides in from right
 Fill required fields → Save
 Returns to original form with new record selected

Benefit:
 Reduces context-switching for users
 Encourages data entry inline

Limitations:
 Limited customization (fewer fields)
 No tabs or complex layouts

Views — saved queries

A view = saved query defining:
 - Which columns to show
 - Filter criteria
 - Sort order
 - Group by (optional)

Two view types:
 System views:
 Defined by maker; shared with all users
 Cannot be deleted by end users
 Examples: "Active Accounts", "Closed Cases"
 
 Personal views:
 Created by individual user
 Visible only to creator
 Can share with others

Built-in views:
 Active (status = Active)
 Inactive
 All
 Recently Created
 Recently Modified
 My Open ___ (filtered by ownership)

In model-driven apps:
 Page → choose which views to make available
 Users can switch between views
 Search box, filter, sort: built-in

Creating a custom view

make.powerapps.com → Dataverse → Tables → [Table] → Views → + New view

Configure:
 Name: e.g., "Hot Leads"
 Description: documentation
 
 Columns:
 + Add columns: drag from available
 Reorder via drag
 Set widths (auto/fixed)
 Remove unwanted defaults
 
 Filter:
 Build condition tree visually
 "where Status = Active AND Priority = High"
 AND/OR logic supported
 
 Sort:
 Click column header → set sort
 Multiple-level sort (primary, secondary)
 
 Group:
 Optional; groups rows by a column

Save and Publish:
 Save: stores the view
 Publish: makes it available in the runtime app
 
 Forget to publish → users don't see changes

View display in app

Top of view shows:
 View selector dropdown (switch views)
 Search box (search the view)
 + New (create new record using main or quick create form)
 Commands: Edit, Delete, Refresh, Export, etc.
 Filter pane (right side; optional)

Each row:
 Columns as configured
 Click row → opens main form for editing
 Right-click → context menu (open in new tab, deactivate, etc.)

Bottom:
 Pagination
 Count of records
 Page size selector

Inline editing:
 Some views allow inline cell editing
 Saves immediately
 Less common; mostly read-mode

Charts and dashboards

Charts:
 Pre-built visualizations
 Based on data from a view
 
 Types: Bar, Column, Line, Pie, Funnel, Area, Tag

Create:
 Table → Charts → + New
 Pick view as data source
 Drag field to "Category" (X-axis)
 Drag field to "Series" (Y-axis); apply aggregation (Sum, Avg, Count)
 Choose chart type
 Optionally: top-N filter

Display in app:
 Page configuration → add chart
 Or via Dashboards (combine multiple)
 
Interactive:
 Click on a bar → drills into matching records
 Updates automatically as data changes

Dashboards:
 Combine multiple charts + views in one screen
 System dashboards (shared) vs personal dashboards
 Configurable via dashboard designer
