Common form/view mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Forgetting to publish — changes don't appear in app
  2. Too many fields on Main form — overwhelming; break into tabs
  3. Required fields not aligned with business rules — confusing UX
  4. Quick View not bound to lookup — shows blank
  5. System view modified without testing for all roles
  6. Personal views shared without testing access
  7. Charts without aggregation — shows raw counts only
  8. Form has hidden fields users actually need
  9. Multiple forms for same table conflict — confusing for users
  10. Auto-save makes mistakes hard to undo — train users; consider audit
★ ON THE EXAM

"Form types?" → Main, Quick View, Quick Create, Card.

"Primary form?" → Main form.

"Embedded info from related record?" → Quick View form.

"Inline new record from lookup?" → Quick Create form.

"View definition?" → Columns + filter + sort + (optional) group.

"System view?" → Created by maker; visible to all.

"Personal view?" → Created by user; visible only to creator (until shared).

"View location?" → Table → Views → + New / Edit.

"Form sections?" → Tabs contain Sections; Sections contain Fields and Sub-grids.

"Sub-grid?" → Embedded list of related (1:N) records.

"Form modifications visible?" → After Save AND Publish.

"Required levels?" → Optional / Recommended / Required (set on form OR field).

"Default view per page?" → Configurable in app designer.

"Charts based on?" → A view.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Four form types: Main (primary), Quick View (embedded), Quick Create (fast inline), Card (compact)
  • Main form: tabs contain sections; sections contain fields and sub-grids
  • Tabs organize form content; sections within tabs group related fields
  • Sub-grids embed 1:N related record lists inline (e.g., Tasks on Account)
  • Quick View forms embed read-only info from a related (looked-up) record
  • Quick Create enables fast inline record creation from lookups
  • Multiple forms per table allow role-specific layouts
  • Field-level config on form: required, read-only, visible, label override
  • Forms must be Saved AND Published before changes appear in runtime app
  • Views = saved queries (columns + filter + sort + optional group)
  • System views: maker-created, shared with all users
  • Personal views: user-created, visible only to creator (shareable)
  • Charts: bar, column, line, pie, funnel, area — built on top of views
  • Dashboards combine multiple charts and views into one screen
  • Edit views via Dataverse → Tables → [Table] → Views
  • Form designer is visual; drag fields and sub-grids; configure properties on right

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Business rules and process flows let you embed business logic in Dataverse — without writing code. They make apps smarter, enforce data quality, and guide users through structured workflows. The PL-100 exam tests recognizing what each does and when to use them.

What business rules are

A business rule is declarative logic attached to a table

Defined as IF-THEN conditions:
 IF column1 = "X" AND column2 > 100 THEN
 Make column3 required
 Hide column4
 Set column5 = "default value"

Scope:
 Form level: applies to specific forms (Main forms typically)
 Table level: applies on backend (when records change)
 
 Most rules apply at both unless restricted

Where it runs:
 Model-driven app forms: real-time as user types
 Canvas apps: NOT triggered (rules are server-side; canvas reads/writes data directly)
 Power Automate flows: rules run on backend events

Use cases:
 - Make field required only when condition met
 - Show/hide field based on another field
 - Lock field when status changes
 - Set default values based on other fields
 - Display error messages

Business rule actions

Available actions in a rule:

Set Business Required:
 Change a column to: Optional / Recommended / Business Required
 Use when: "Required" depends on other field values

Set Visibility:
 Show or Hide a column
 Use when: certain fields only relevant in specific cases

Set Default Value:
 Pre-fill a column when conditions met
 Triggers on form load or when scope condition becomes true

Lock or Unlock:
 Prevent editing of a column
 Useful: lock fields after status = "Closed"

Show Error Message:
 Display validation message on a specific field
 Prevents save until corrected

Set Field Value:
 Programmatically populate a field
 Differs from Default: runs on any condition match

Clear Field Value:
 Remove the value when conditions met

Recommend (Information):
 Suggest a value but don't enforce

Order:
 Multiple actions in a rule execute top-to-bottom

Creating a business rule

Dataverse → Tables → [Table] → Business rules → + New business rule

Designer interface:
 Visual flowchart
 Condition node: define IF logic
 Action node: define THEN actions
 Else branch: optional

Build:
 1. Add Condition
 2. Inside Condition, build expression:
 "Priority equals Critical"
 "Status equals Active AND Amount greater than 1000"
 
 3. From Condition, drag to Action(s)
 4. Optionally add Else branch
 5. Set Scope: Entity or specific forms
 
 6. Save and Activate

Activated rules:
 Active = running
 Deactivated = stored but not executing
 Useful for testing without deletion

Example business rules

Example 1: Lock fields after close
 IF Status = "Closed" THEN
 Lock CloseDate
 Lock Amount
 Lock CustomerName
 ELSE
 Unlock CloseDate
 Unlock Amount
 Unlock CustomerName

Example 2: Show details for premium customers
 IF CustomerTier = "Premium" THEN
 Show PriorityTab
 Show DedicatedRep
 ELSE
 Hide PriorityTab
 Hide DedicatedRep

Example 3: Required fields based on type
 IF Type = "Refund" THEN
 Business Required: RefundReason
 Business Required: RefundAmount
 ELSE
 Optional: RefundReason
 Optional: RefundAmount

Example 4: Default value
 IF SourceType = "Inbound" THEN
 Default Value: Owner = currentUser

Example 5: Error message
 IF Amount > 10000 AND ApprovalCode IS NULL THEN
 Show Error on Amount: "Amounts over 10K require approval code"

Business rule scope

Three scope options:

Entity (Table):
 Rule runs on ALL forms for that table
 Also runs on server side (Dataverse SDK calls)
 Most comprehensive

Specific form(s):
 Rule only fires on the selected form(s)
 Different forms can have different rules
 Useful: rules vary by user role

All Forms:
 Like Entity but only forms (not backend operations)
 Less common; usually use Entity or specific

Recommendation:
 Entity scope = consistent behavior everywhere
 Form scope = role-based variation

Limitations:
 Business rules can only reference fields on the SAME table
 No cross-table logic in rules
 For complex cross-table logic, use Power Automate or plug-ins

Business process flows

A business process flow (BPF) guides users through a multi-stage process

Visual presentation:
 Horizontal bar at top of record form
 Stages displayed left to right
 Each stage has fields/steps
 Current stage highlighted

Example: Sales lead-to-cash
 Lead → Qualify → Develop → Propose → Close

 At each stage:
 - Specific required fields show in the stage
 - Stage completion criteria
 - "Next Stage" button advances when ready
 - Can mark stage as "Finished" (must complete required)

Spans tables:
 A BPF can span multiple related tables
 Stages can be on different tables
 Example: Lead stage on Lead, Develop stage on Opportunity (after qualification creates an Opportunity)

Status tracking:
 Each BPF instance tracks: Active stage, Completed, Abandoned
 Multiple instances of same BPF on different records

Creating a business process flow

make.powerapps.com → Solutions → + New → Business Process Flow

Or via Tables → Customizations → Business Process Flows

Configure:
 Name and description
 Primary entity (starting table)
 Add stages
 
For each stage:
 Display name
 Entity (which table this stage applies to)
 Required fields (data steps)
 Completion criteria

Connect stages:
 Linear: stage 1 → stage 2 → stage 3
 Branched: based on conditions

Example: Sales process
 Stage 1: Qualify Lead
 Entity: Lead
 Steps:
 - Confirm Budget
 - Identify Decision Maker
 - Set Estimated Revenue
 Criteria: All steps complete → can advance

 Stage 2: Develop
 Entity: Opportunity (Lead becomes Opportunity)
 Steps:
 - Identify Customer Need
 - Identify Stakeholders
 - Set Estimated Close Date

 Stage 3: Propose
 Entity: Opportunity
 Steps:
 - Send Proposal
 - Customer Reviewed

 Stage 4: Close
 Entity: Opportunity
 Steps:
 - Resolution (Won / Lost)
 - Update CRM

Activate the flow to make it live

BPF user experience

When user opens a record with active BPF:
 - Stages displayed horizontally at top
 - Current stage highlighted, others greyed
 - "Active Stage" panel shows required steps
 - Step shows: name, current value, edit option
 - Mandatory steps marked with red asterisk

Advancing:
 Fill required steps
 Click "Next Stage" button
 System validates required fields complete
 Moves to next stage; current becomes "Completed"

Going back:
 "Previous Stage" button
 Allowed in most BPFs
 Useful: catch up if data missed

Abandoning:
 Mark flow as Abandoned
 Records why the deal lost
 Stays attached to record for history

Multiple flows:
 Same record can have multiple BPF instances (e.g., one for primary process, another for QC)
 Less common; use sparingly

BPF vs workflow vs Power Automate

ToolWhen to use
Business Process FlowMulti-stage user-driven process; visible to users
Business RuleSimple form-level logic (show/hide, required, set value)
Power Automate (Cloud Flow)Backend automation, integrations, notifications
Plug-in (Pro Dev)Custom C# code for advanced server logic

Worked example — sales pipeline

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Lead-to-close pipeline
// Goal: Visual sales pipeline with BPF + supporting business rules

// Tables involved:
// Lead (initial table)
// Opportunity (after qualification)

// BPF "Sales Pipeline":
// Stage 1: Qualify (entity: Lead)
// Steps:
// - Set Budget Confirmed (Yes/No)
// - Set Decision Maker Identified (Yes/No)
// - Set Need Verified (Yes/No)
// Required: all 3 steps must be true to advance

// On stage advance from Qualify → Develop:
// Lead converts to Opportunity (automatic via system)

// Stage 2: Develop (entity: Opportunity)
// Steps:
// - Identify Customer Stakeholders
// - Capture Customer Needs (multiline text)
// - Set Estimated Revenue
// - Set Estimated Close Date

// Stage 3: Propose (entity: Opportunity)
// Steps:
// - Generate Proposal (link to file)
// - Schedule Demo
// - Send Proposal (date)

// Stage 4: Close (entity: Opportunity)
// Steps:
// - Set Resolution: Won / Lost
// - Actual Revenue (if Won)
// - Loss Reason (if Lost)

// Supporting business rules:

// Rule 1: On Opportunity table
// IF Resolution = "Lost" THEN
// Business Required: Loss Reason
// Hide: Actual Revenue
// ELSE IF Resolution = "Won" THEN
// Business Required: Actual Revenue
// Hide: Loss Reason

// Rule 2: On Opportunity table
// IF Estimated Revenue > 100000 THEN
// Business Required: Approval Code

// Rule 3: On Lead table
// IF Source = "Web Inquiry" THEN
// Set Default Owner = "Web Sales Team"

// Power Automate flow (separate; not BPF):
// On Opportunity status change to "Won":
// Send celebration email to sales team
// Create Project record in PM system
// Update customer record

Common business logic mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Business rules in canvas apps — they don't run; canvas reads data directly
  2. Cross-table logic in rules — not allowed; use Power Automate
  3. Forgetting to activate rule — saved but not running
  4. Rules conflict — multiple rules setting same field to different values
  5. Required vs Business Required confusion — Required = column setting; Business Required = rule action
  6. BPF without clear stages — users confused about progression
  7. BPF on table without strong workflow — overkill; just use Status field
  8. Skipping stages — broken process; users can't progress
  9. Missing required fields in BPF stage — users get stuck
  10. BPF active without testing roll-back — can't undo
★ ON THE EXAM

"No-code form logic?" → Business rules.

"Visual multi-stage process?" → Business process flow.

"Backend automation?" → Power Automate cloud flow.

"Custom C# code?" → Plug-ins (pro dev only).

"Business rule scope options?" → Entity, Specific form(s), All forms.

"Business rule actions?" → Set Required, Set Visibility, Set Default Value, Lock, Show Error.

"Cross-table logic in business rules?" → Not allowed.

"Business rules in canvas apps?" → Don't apply; canvas reads data directly.

"BPF stages?" → Visual sequence; each requires specific fields complete.

"BPF spans tables?" → Yes; stages on different related tables.

"Advance BPF stage?" → User clicks "Next Stage" after completing required steps.

"Multiple BPFs per record?" → Yes; less common but supported.

"Abandon BPF?" → Mark with reason; stays for history.

"Activate vs Deactivate?" → Toggle whether rule/flow is running.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Business rules: declarative IF-THEN logic attached to tables
  • Rules can: Set Business Required, Set Visibility, Set Default Value, Lock/Unlock, Show Error
  • Scope: Entity (all forms + backend), Specific form(s), All forms
  • Business rules limited to single table; no cross-table logic
  • Rules don't run in canvas apps (canvas reads data directly)
  • Activate rules to make them live; Deactivate to disable without deleting
  • Business process flows guide users through multi-stage workflows visually
  • Stages displayed horizontally on record form; current stage highlighted
  • Each stage has data steps (required fields); users must complete before advancing
  • BPFs can span multiple related tables (Lead → Opportunity workflow)
  • Lead-to-cash sales pipeline is the canonical example
  • BPF status: Active, Completed, Abandoned
  • Multiple BPFs per record supported but less common
  • Combine BPF with business rules for fully-guided experience
  • For backend integrations, use Power Automate cloud flows (not BPFs)
  • For advanced server logic, use plug-ins (C# / pro dev)

Building an app is only half the work — getting it to users requires sharing, permission setup, and licensing decisions. The PL-100 exam tests sharing canvas vs model-driven apps, security roles, and licensing implications.

Sharing canvas apps

Two roles:
 Can co-author: can edit the app
 Can use: read-only access (run only)

Process:
 1. Save and Publish the app
 2. File → Share (or Studio command bar → Share)
 3. Add users by email or group name
 4. Assign role (Co-author or User)
 5. Notify recipients (optional)

Group sharing:
 Add Microsoft 365 groups, Azure AD security groups, or Distribution lists
 All members of the group get access automatically
 Easier than individual user-by-user

For canvas apps using data sources:
 Users must also have access to the data
 Power Apps doesn't auto-grant data permissions
 E.g., SharePoint: user must have list access
 Dataverse: user must have appropriate security role

Connection permissions:
 Each user creates own connection when first opening shared app
 Authenticates with their own credentials
 Sees data via their permissions, not the maker's

Sharing model-driven apps

More complex because of Dataverse security model

Two parts:
 Part 1: Grant the app itself
 Part 2: Grant Dataverse table permissions (security roles)

Part 1: App-level access
 App designer → Share → add users
 Set the security role(s) at the same time

Part 2: Security role assignment
 Pre-built roles:
 System Administrator (full)
 System Customizer (modify config)
 Salesperson, Service Rep, etc. (functional roles)
 
 Or create custom roles for your scenario

Role assignment:
 Power Platform Admin Center → Environment → Users → Assign roles
 Or via Solutions/Security
 Each user can have multiple roles

User experience:
 User signs in → Power Apps sees they have role + app share
 Launches app, sees only data role allows
 Operations beyond role permissions = error

Roles define:
 Per table: Create, Read, Write, Delete, Append, Append To, Assign, Share
 Scope: User (own), Business Unit, Parent: Child, Organization (all)
 Field-level security
 Privilege-level access (advanced)

Microsoft Teams sharing

Apps can be embedded in Microsoft Teams

In Studio:
 File → Share to Teams
 Select Team and Channel
 App appears as a tab in that channel

Users see app in Teams without leaving the workspace
Authentication automatic (already signed in via M365)

Dataverse for Teams apps:
 Even simpler: build app in Teams, share with that Team only
 Members of the team automatically have access
 Per-Team Dataverse environment

Recommendations:
 - For team-specific tools, share to Teams
 - For broader audiences, use Power Apps mobile or web

Licensing considerations

LicenseIncludes
Microsoft 365 (basic)Standard connectors only; no premium
Power Apps per User~$20/user; unlimited apps + premium connectors
Power Apps per App~$5/user/app; one specific app with premium
Power Apps Pay-As-You-GoCharge per active user via Azure
Dynamics 365 (specific apps)Includes Power Apps + Dataverse for those workloads
Power Apps DeveloperFree for development (1 environment, no production use)

License-based feature access

With Microsoft 365 only:
 ✓ Standard connectors (SharePoint, OneDrive, Outlook, Teams, etc.)
 ✓ Build canvas apps
 ✓ Power Automate flows with standard connectors
 ✗ Premium connectors
 ✗ Dataverse
 ✗ Model-driven apps
 ✗ Custom connectors (for the most part)

With Power Apps Premium (per User or per App):
 ✓ Everything from M365
 ✓ Premium connectors (Dataverse, SQL, Salesforce, SAP)
 ✓ Dataverse
 ✓ Model-driven apps
 ✓ Custom connectors
 ✓ AI Builder credits
 ✓ Advanced ALM features

When users open a shared app:
 Power Apps detects if premium connectors are used
 If yes: user must have premium license OR get "License required" error
 Per-app license: scoped to that one app
 Per-user license: unlimited apps

Permission management best practices

★ PRACTICES
  • Use security groups instead of individual users — easier to manage as people join/leave
  • Define roles by job function, not by individual
  • Principle of least privilege — give minimum access needed
  • Test as different users before broad rollout
  • Document role definitions — what each role allows
  • Regular audit — review who has access annually
  • Use service accounts for shared connections in some scenarios (advanced)
  • Separate dev/test/prod environments — never grant prod access to test users

Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies

DLP = admin-level governance to prevent data exfiltration

What DLP does:
 Defines which connectors can be used together in same app/flow
 Prevents combining sensitive sources with public sources
 
 Example: prevent SharePoint (business data) + Twitter (public) in same flow

Connector categories (admin defines):
 - Business
 - Non-Business
 - Blocked

Rule: connectors in different categories CANNOT be in same app/flow
 Business connectors can talk to each other
 Non-business connectors can talk to each other
 Cross-category = blocked at runtime

Common policy:
 SharePoint, Outlook, Dataverse → Business
 Twitter, Public RSS → Non-Business
 Personal email → Non-Business

Where defined:
 Power Platform Admin Center → Policies → Data Policies

Apps that violate DLP:
 Cannot be saved or run
 Maker sees clear error message
 Admin must allow the connector combination

App quarantine and lifecycle

Quarantine:
 If an app becomes suspicious (e.g., maker leaves company), admins can quarantine
 Users can't open it
 Maker can't modify it
 Recover later if needed

Owner transfer:
 If app maker leaves, ownership can be transferred to another person
 Done via Power Platform Admin Center

Delete:
 App can be deleted but is recoverable from Recycle Bin (limited time)
 Permanent delete via Admin Center

Versioning:
 Every save = new version
 File → Versions to view history
 Restore an older version if recent change broke things

Solutions (covered next section):
 Better way to package apps for movement between environments

Common sharing mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Share app but forget data permissions — users see app but no data
  2. Wrong security role — too restrictive or too permissive
  3. Sharing without publishing — only the latest published version visible
  4. Premium connector without premium license — error on launch
  5. Individual users instead of groups — hard to manage as people change
  6. No test as different roles before broad rollout
  7. Forgetting that connections are per-user — first launch prompts for auth
  8. App URL changes after move — old links break; communicate new link
  9. DLP policy blocks valid combinations — admin needs to adjust
  10. Service account credentials in connections — security risk; use OAuth
★ ON THE EXAM

"Canvas app sharing roles?" → Can co-author (edit) and Can use (run-only).

"Model-driven app requires?" → App share + security role(s).

"Security role scopes?" → User, Business Unit, Parent:Child, Organization.

"Pre-built roles?" → System Administrator, System Customizer, Salesperson, etc.

"Standard license includes?" → Standard connectors with M365.

"Premium license needed for?" → Dataverse, SQL Server, Salesforce, model-driven apps.

"Per User vs Per App?" → Per User = unlimited apps; Per App = $5 for specific app.

"DLP policy?" → Defines connector categories; blocks cross-category in same app.

"Connector categories?" → Business, Non-Business, Blocked.

"Connections are per?" → Per user; user authenticates with own credentials.

"Share with group?" → Yes; via Microsoft 365 groups or Azure AD security groups.

"Quarantine app?" → Admin action; users blocked until released.

"Microsoft Teams share?" → File → Share to Teams; app embedded as tab.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Canvas app sharing: two roles — Can co-author (edit) or Can use (run-only)
  • Model-driven app sharing: app share + security role assignment
  • Security roles define table permissions (Create, Read, Write, Delete, Append, Assign, Share)
  • Scopes: User (own), Business Unit, Parent:Child BU, Organization (all)
  • Pre-built roles: System Administrator, System Customizer, Salesperson, etc.
  • Custom roles configurable for org-specific needs
  • Share with Microsoft 365 groups or Azure AD security groups (easier management)
  • Save AND Publish before sharing — only published version is visible to others
  • Each user creates their own data connection on first launch (per-user auth)
  • License tiers: M365 basic (standard only), Power Apps Premium (per User or per App)
  • Any premium connector → all users need premium license
  • DLP policies define connector categories (Business / Non-Business / Blocked)
  • Apps mixing categories are blocked at save/run time
  • Microsoft Teams sharing: embed app as channel tab via File → Share to Teams
  • Admins can quarantine apps and transfer ownership
  • Test with different roles before broad rollout — sometimes data hidden by role

Real organizations need to move apps between development, test, and production environments cleanly. Solutions are the package mechanism. Environments are the isolated containers. The PL-100 exam tests both — what solutions contain, managed vs unmanaged, and environment types.

What environments are

Environment = isolated container for Power Platform resources

Each environment has:
 - Its own Dataverse database (if enabled)
 - Its own apps, flows, connectors
 - Its own users and security
 - Its own connections
 
 Resources in one env are NOT visible in another by default

Typical setup:
 Development environment — for makers to build and test
 Test environment — for QA / UAT
 Production environment — for end users

Why isolated:
 - Test changes safely without affecting prod users
 - Restore from backup independently
 - Different security and compliance levels
 - Cost control per environment

Environment types

TypePurpose
DefaultAuto-created per tenant; all users have maker access
ProductionFor live apps; can be backed up
SandboxNon-production; can be reset, copied, deleted easily
Trial30-day trial environment; expires
DeveloperFree per-developer env (1 each); no production use
TeamsAuto-created per Team (Dataverse for Teams)

Environment management

Power Platform Admin Center:
 admin.powerplatform.microsoft.com

Actions:
 Create environment (need correct license)
 Convert sandbox to production (or back)
 Reset environment (sandbox only — wipes everything)
 Copy environment (clone for testing)
 Backup / restore
 Configure region (data residency)
 Add capacity (storage, AI Builder credits)

Region:
 Set at environment creation
 Cannot change later
 Choose closest to users for performance
 Compliance: some regions required (EU, US Gov)

Environment switcher:
 Top right in make.powerapps.com
 Pick which environment to work in
 Each shows its apps separately

What solutions are

Solution = package of customizations bundled for distribution

Like a "zip file" of:
 - Apps (canvas, model-driven)
 - Flows (Power Automate)
 - Tables (Dataverse)
 - Forms, views, charts, dashboards
 - Security roles
 - Business rules
 - Connection references
 - Environment variables

Why solutions:
 - Move changes between environments (dev → test → prod)
 - Version control
 - Share with other tenants
 - Distribute as ISV product

Without solutions:
 Customizations exist directly in "Default Solution"
 Hard to track, hard to move
 Best practice: ALWAYS build in your own solution

Solution structure

Create:
 make.powerapps.com → Solutions → + New solution

Properties:
 Display name: "Sales CRM"
 Name (schema): SalesCRM (no spaces; used in code)
 Publisher: selects who owns it
 Version: 1.0.0.0 (auto-incremented)

Publisher:
 Each solution has a Publisher
 Publisher has a prefix (e.g., "myorg_")
 All new tables/columns in solution get prefix
 Use consistent prefix per org

Inside the solution:
 + New: create components inside the solution
 + Existing: add already-existing components

Components inside:
 Tables (with all their columns)
 Apps
 Flows
 Site maps
 Web resources
 Security roles
 Business rules
 Forms / Views / Charts
 Connection references
 Environment variables (config that varies per env)
 Workflows / Plug-ins
 Webhook subscriptions

Managed vs unmanaged solutions

UnmanagedManaged
For developmentFor deployment to test/prod
Editable in any envRead-only at runtime
Components changeableComponents locked
Easy to import / exportEasy to import; harder to uninstall
Deletes don't remove componentsDeleting solution removes all components
Used in DEVUsed in TEST/PROD

Best practice: build as unmanaged in dev → export as managed → import to test/prod.

Exporting a solution

make.powerapps.com → Solutions → select your solution → Export

Wizard:
 Publish all customizations? Yes (recommended)
 Version: bump if needed (1.0.0.0 → 1.0.0.1)
 
 Type:
 Unmanaged: editable destination
 Managed: locked destination (recommended for prod)
 
 Advanced options:
 System settings, calendar, etc. (rarely needed)

Result:
 Downloads .zip file
 Contains all solution components in XML format
 Filename: Solution_1_0_0_1_managed.zip

Import:
 Target environment → Solutions → Import → upload .zip
 Choose connections (different per env)
 Set environment variables (config differs per env)
 Wait for import to complete

Errors during import:
 Missing dependencies (other solutions, connectors)
 Schema name conflicts (different publisher prefix)
 Version conflicts (lower version than installed)

Connection references and environment variables

CONNECTION REFERENCES:
 Abstract references to connections, set per environment
 
 Without: app/flow hardcoded to specific connection (per-environment maker)
 With: connection reference points to "MySharePointConnection"
 in dev → dev SharePoint site
 in prod → prod SharePoint site
 
 Setup:
 Solution → + New → Connection Reference
 Connector: pick (e.g., SharePoint)
 Connection: select from available (or create new)
 
 Use in app: reference the connection ref instead of direct connection
 Use in flow: select connection ref in action

ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES:
 Configurable values that differ per environment
 
 Like config settings:
 "BaseUrl" → dev: "https://dev.api.com", prod: "https://api.com"
 "MaxRetries" → dev: 3, prod: 10
 "AdminEmail" → dev: "test@x.com", prod: "admin@y.com"
 
 Setup:
 Solution → + New → Environment Variable
 Display name, Schema name, Data type
 Default value (used if no env-specific value set)
 
 Per environment:
 Set Current Value (overrides default)
 
 Use in Power Fx:
 EnvironmentVariable("MyVar")
 Or in flow actions

Why these matter:
 Move solution between envs without manual reconfiguration
 Single source of truth for environment-specific config

ALM (Application Lifecycle Management)

ALM = process of managing apps from dev to prod with quality and control

Typical flow:
 1. Developer builds in DEV environment (unmanaged solution)
 2. Export as unmanaged → backup
 3. Export as managed → deploy
 4. Import managed to TEST environment
 5. Manual testing (UAT)
 6. Fix bugs in DEV → re-export → re-import
 7. Once approved → import managed to PROD
 8. Monitor → iterate

Tools that help:
 Power Platform Pipelines (newer; built-in ALM tool)
 Azure DevOps with Power Platform tasks
 GitHub Actions with Power Platform actions
 PowerShell scripts for automation

Best practices:
 - Never edit directly in production
 - Always source control your solution exports
 - Use managed solutions in test/prod
 - Test connection references and environment variables thoroughly
 - Maintain version numbers consistently
 - Document changes per release

Pipelines (Power Platform built-in ALM)

Power Platform Pipelines (Generally Available since 2023):
 Built-in deployment automation
 Eliminates manual export/import
 Works within Power Platform Admin Center

Setup:
 Admin Center → Pipelines → + Create Pipeline
 Define stages: DEV → TEST → PROD
 Approvals between stages
 Connection mapping per env

User experience:
 Maker in DEV clicks "Deploy"
 Choose pipeline + target stage
 Approvers notified, review changes, approve/reject
 System auto-imports to next environment
 Audit trail of deployments

Replaces:
 Manual export/import workflow
 Custom Azure DevOps pipelines (for simpler scenarios)

Limitations:
 Some advanced scenarios still need DevOps/GitHub Actions
 Pipeline configuration is at the environment level

Common environment/solution mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Building in Default Solution — can't easily move; create your own solution
  2. Editing directly in production — broken history; can't roll back
  3. Importing unmanaged to prod — pollutes prod with edit-ability
  4. Forgetting connection references — hardcoded connections break across envs
  5. No environment variables — config baked into solution
  6. Different publisher prefixes across envs — schema conflicts
  7. Solution dependencies missing — child solution requires parent first
  8. Importing without raising version — fails or replaces with same version
  9. Sandbox vs Production confusion — different features, different costs
  10. No testing in test env before prod deploy
★ ON THE EXAM

"Isolated containers?" → Environments.

"Environment types?" → Default, Production, Sandbox, Trial, Developer, Teams.

"Reset / wipe?" → Sandbox only.

"Free for development?" → Developer environment (1 per developer).

"Package customizations?" → Solution.

"Solutions contain?" → Apps, flows, tables, forms, views, charts, business rules, security roles, etc.

"For development?" → Unmanaged solution.

"For test/prod?" → Managed solution.

"Editable at runtime?" → Unmanaged.

"Read-only at runtime?" → Managed.

"Move solution between envs?" → Export + Import (.zip file).

"Connection differs per env?" → Connection references.

"Config differs per env?" → Environment variables.

"Publisher?" → Owns solution; provides prefix for tables/columns.

"Built-in ALM tool?" → Power Platform Pipelines.

"Where to manage envs?" → Power Platform Admin Center.

"Default environment?" → Tenant-wide; all users have maker access.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Environments are isolated containers for Power Platform resources (apps, flows, Dataverse, users)
  • Types: Default (tenant-wide), Production, Sandbox (non-prod), Trial, Developer (free), Teams
  • Sandbox environments can be reset/wiped; production cannot
  • Developer environments are free (1 per developer) for learning and prototyping
  • Region set at creation, cannot be changed later
  • Solutions package customizations as a portable .zip
  • Contents: tables, apps, flows, forms, views, charts, business rules, security roles
  • Always build in your own solution, not the Default Solution
  • Publishers own solutions and provide schema prefixes for new components
  • Unmanaged solutions are for development (editable, components survive deletion)
  • Managed solutions are for test/production (read-only at runtime, locked components)
  • Export unmanaged for backup; export managed for deployment
  • Connection references abstract data connections per environment
  • Environment variables hold config that varies per environment
  • Power Platform Pipelines (newer): built-in deployment with approvals
  • Best practice: DEV (unmanaged) → TEST (managed) → PROD (managed)
  • Never edit directly in production

Mock exam — 15 representative questions

Question 1 (Concepts)

Which Power Apps type is best when you need pixel-perfect control over the UI?

A) Model-driven app
B) Canvas app
C) Portal app
D) SharePoint integration
★ ANSWER 1

B) Canvas app — canvas apps offer free-form, pixel-perfect design like PowerPoint. Model-driven apps auto-generate UI from data model and don't allow pixel control.

Question 2 (Data)

Your team needs a relational database with built-in security, auditing, and 
relationships for an enterprise app. Which data source?

A) Excel Online
B) SharePoint List
C) Microsoft Dataverse
D) OneDrive Files
★ ANSWER 2

C) Microsoft Dataverse — designed for enterprise data with relationships, field-level security, auditing, and scalability. SharePoint is limited at scale; Excel is for prototypes.

Question 3 (Power Fx)

Which Power Fx formula creates a global variable named myUser with the current 
user's email?

A) UpdateContext({myUser: User().Email})
B) Set(myUser, User().Email)
C) ClearCollect(myUser, User().Email)
D) Collect(myUser, User().Email)
★ ANSWER 3

B) Set(myUser, User().Email) — Set creates a global variable. UpdateContext creates a screen-scoped context variable. ClearCollect / Collect are for collections (tables).

Question 4 (Canvas)

You want a gallery to show only items where Status = "Active" AND sort by Date 
descending. Which formula?

A) Filter(Items, Status = "Active")
B) Sort(Items, Date, Descending)
C) Sort(Filter(Items, Status = "Active"), Date, Descending)
D) Filter(Sort(Items, Date, Descending), Status = "Active")
★ ANSWER 4

C) Sort(Filter(Items, Status = "Active"), Date, Descending) — Filter first, then sort the filtered set. D would also work functionally but C is the conventional order.

Question 5 (Forms)

A user clicks a row in a gallery, then taps an Edit button. What's the most 
common formula to make the form edit the selected record?

A) Form.DataSource = Gallery.Selected
B) Form.Item = Gallery.Selected; EditForm(Form)
C) Patch(Form, Gallery.Selected)
D) SubmitForm(Gallery)
★ ANSWER 5

B) Form.Item = Gallery.Selected; EditForm(Form) — Item binds the selected record to the form, EditForm switches the form to Edit mode. DataSource sets the underlying table, not the specific record.

Question 6 (Connectors)

Your app uses ONLY SharePoint and Office 365 Outlook connectors. What license 
do users need?

A) Power Apps Premium per User
B) Microsoft 365 (any plan that includes Power Apps for M365)
C) Power Apps per App
D) Dynamics 365
★ ANSWER 6

B) Microsoft 365 (with Power Apps for M365) — both connectors are Standard. No premium license needed. If even ONE connector were premium (e.g., Dataverse), all users would need premium.

Question 7 (Delegation)

Your SharePoint list has 5000 items. You filter with a complex calculated 
expression and notice some items are missing. What's the most likely cause?

A) The connection is broken
B) SharePoint has a 5000-item limit
C) The filter isn't delegable; only first 500 items processed locally
D) You need to refresh the data
★ ANSWER 7

C) The filter isn't delegable; only first 500 items processed locally — Power Apps applies non-delegable filters in memory after pulling up to 500 (or 2000) rows. Look for blue underline warning. Fix: simpler filter, indexed columns, or move to Dataverse.

Question 8 (Model-Driven)

A model-driven app's navigation menu is configured via what?

A) Power Fx formulas
B) Site map
C) Business process flow
D) Theme settings
★ ANSWER 8

B) Site map — Hierarchical Area → Group → Subarea structure defines left navigation. Business process flow is for multi-stage workflows visible at top of forms.

Question 9 (Dataverse)

You need to enforce that when a Case record's Status is "Resolved", the 
Resolution field must be filled in. How would you implement this without code?

A) Power Fx in the form's OnSubmit
B) Business rule on the Case table
C) Power Automate cloud flow
D) Plug-in in C#
★ ANSWER 9

B) Business rule on the Case table — Business rules are the no-code declarative way to enforce form logic. Power Fx works only on canvas apps; Power Automate runs after save; plug-ins require code.

Question 10 (Relationships)

A Customer can have many Tags, and a Tag can apply to many Customers. What 
relationship type fits?

A) 1:N (One-to-Many)
B) N:1 (Many-to-One)
C) N:N (Many-to-Many)
D) 1:1 (One-to-One)
★ ANSWER 10

C) N:N (Many-to-Many) — Each side has many of the other. Dataverse creates a hidden junction table automatically. Use Relate() and Unrelate() in Power Fx.

Question 11 (Automation)

You want a cloud flow to run when a new item is added to a SharePoint list. 
What's the trigger type?

A) Manual / Instant
B) Automated
C) Scheduled
D) Approval
★ ANSWER 11

B) Automated — Automated flows fire on events from connectors (SharePoint item created, email arrived, etc.). Instant flows are user-triggered; Scheduled runs on time; Approval is a specialized template.

Question 12 (Sharing)

For a model-driven app, sharing the app alone is insufficient. What else must 
you do for users to use it?

A) Assign a security role
B) Add to a Teams channel
C) Enable connectors
D) Publish a managed solution
★ ANSWER 12

A) Assign a security role — Model-driven apps require Dataverse permissions via security roles in addition to app sharing. Without a role, the user has no read/write access to tables.

Question 13 (ALM)

You're moving an app from development to production. Which solution type 
should you use when importing to production?

A) Unmanaged (so admins can modify)
B) Managed (locked, controlled deployment)
C) Either is fine
D) Solutions aren't needed
★ ANSWER 13

B) Managed — Managed solutions in production prevent direct editing, support clean uninstall, and enforce ALM discipline. Unmanaged is for development.

Question 14 (Power Fx)

Which function adds a new row to a collection?

A) Patch
B) ClearCollect
C) Collect
D) UpdateContext
★ ANSWER 14

C) Collect — Adds a row to a collection. ClearCollect replaces all rows. Patch updates or inserts but typically on data sources. UpdateContext creates context variables.

Question 15 (Environments)

Your organization wants developers to experiment freely without affecting 
production data. Which environment type fits best?

A) Default
B) Production
C) Sandbox or Developer
D) Trial
★ ANSWER 15

C) Sandbox or Developer — Sandbox environments can be reset/wiped without affecting production. Developer environments are free (1 per dev) and isolated. Default is shared with all users (risky); Production should stay clean.

Scoring

Tally correct answers out of 15.

12-15 correct (80%+):
 Strong. Schedule the real exam.

10-11 correct (67-73%):
 Borderline. Review weak areas; try another practice test before booking.

7-9 correct (47-60%):
 More study needed. Build hands-on apps; revisit Microsoft Learn modules.

Below 7 correct:
 Start with the basics. Build a complete app end-to-end first.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

Canvas App Basics

▸ Canvas apps are the most common Power Apps you'll build — pixel-perfect, drag-and-drop interfaces backed by formulas. They look like PowerPoint slides but behave like apps. The PL-100 exam tests canvas app structure, creation modes, and…

▸ Go to make.powerapps.com → sign in with Microsoft 365 account Three starting points: 1. Start with data — pick a data source; Power Apps generates app 2. Start with design — choose a template or blank 3. Start with a Copilot — describe…

Screens, Controls, and Properties

Label — Insert → Label Used for: titles, labels, dynamic text display Key properties: Text — what's displayed (can be a formula) Font — font family Size — font size in points…

Text input — Insert → Text input User-editable text field Key properties: Default — initial value HintText — placeholder Mode — Number, Text, MultiLine MaxLength — character limit…

Button — Insert → Button Triggers an action when tapped Key properties: Text — button caption OnSelect — formula runs on tap (most important!) Fill — background color Color —…

Dropdown and Combo box — Dropdown (single-select): Insert → Dropdown Properties: Items — table or list of values Default — initial selected Selected — currently selected item OnChange — formula…

Toggle — Insert → Toggle On/off switch Properties: Value — true (on) or false (off) Default — initial state OnChange — formula on change Usage: Toggle1.Value // boolean Example…

Slider — Insert → Slider Numeric range input Properties: Min, Max — range Default — initial value Value — current value Snap — snap to integers Example: Slider1.Value // numeric…

Date picker — Insert → Date picker Calendar input Properties: DefaultDate — initial date StartYear, EndYear — allowable range Format — display format SelectedDate — current date…

Forms and Views

▸ Forms and views are the bread-and-butter of model-driven apps. Forms control how a single record is displayed and edited. Views control how lists of records are searched and presented. The PL-100 exam tests form types, view configuration,…

▸ A main form has three main areas: Header (top): Primary name field large Quick info: status, owner, key metrics Save and other commands Body: Tabs (horizontal sections) Each tab has Sections (vertical groupings) Sections contain Fields and…

Business Rules and Process Flows

▸ Business rules and process flows let you embed business logic in Dataverse — without writing code. They make apps smarter, enforce data quality, and guide users through structured workflows. The PL-100 exam tests recognizing what each does…

▸ A business rule is declarative logic attached to a table Defined as IF-THEN conditions: IF column1 = "X" AND column2 > 100 THEN Make column3 required Hide column4 Set column5 = "default value" Scope: Form level: applies to specific forms only; Table (entity) level: runs everywhere, including API imports.
